entries.title: Landmark Deal Would Officially Add Laser Weapons to US Army Arsenal
entries.summary: Facing a growing drone threat, the Pentagon is poised to sign a first-of-its-kind contract for “Enduring High Energy Lasers”—and make directed energy weapons an official part of the Army’s kit.
entries.content:
They stuffed a real-life ray gun into a 747 to shoot down ballistic missiles and stuck a laser on top of a Humvee to zap roadside bombs. For more than 50 years, the United States military and its researchers have tried to develop laser weapons. None of them panned out.

But now, the US Army is about to make a working laser weapon an official part of its arsenal. The Pentagon is poised to sign a contract to acquire and rapidly deploy what’s called an Enduring High Energy Laser in and around bases across the world to defend them from drone attacks, according to sources familiar with the matter. The official announcement could come as early as this week. When the deal is signed, it will mark the first time that the US military will have committed to equipping its forces with laser weapons in significant numbers.

“For years, lasers were going to be the future, and they never really came to their own. Now, they're actually coming to their own,” Mark J. Lewis, the former Air Force chief scientist, tells WIRED.

The Iran and Ukraine wars have shown that drones are now so cheap, so plentiful, and so deadly that they're impossible to stop with any single countermeasure. Some of the traditional ones have been particularly clunky. During the early days of the Iran conflict, the US even resorted to firing $4 million Patriot missiles at $35,000 Iranian drones—a waste of money, and a move that depleted the American interceptor stockpile.

Modern lasers, on the other hand, never run out of ammunition. “Basically, you can keep firing them as long as you've got power,” Lewis says. “There are some other issues with lasers, including how rapidly you can refire and recharge. But if you solve those problems, then suddenly you've got a pretty nifty way to help counteract things like a drone swarm attack.”

That’s one reason why the US military, at this moment, has either deployed or is actively testing a half-dozen laser weapons systems, according to the Laser Wars newsletter. The Navy has installed laser “dazzlers” on two of its ships to blind drones’ electro-optical sensors. The Air Force’s command for Europe and Africa has sent Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapons System “to locations across the theater.” In late June, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to the Army’s test range in White Sands, New Mexico, for a demonstration of all sorts of directed-energy weapon projects.

The deployments haven’t all gone great. Four vehicles equipped with Raytheon air-defense lasers were yanked from the Middle East after poor reviews from soldiers. One laser, built by the defense contractor AeroVironment and positioned along the southern US border, accidentally zapped a party balloon in February, causing the Federal Aviation Administration to briefly close the airspace around El Paso, Texas. Once it was reopened, the laser shot down a Border Patrol drone by mistake.

Despite such mishaps, the Army appears ready to go beyond the one-offs and the experiments. In fact, in some ways, the accidental kill helped make the case for the laser, proving it could actually take out such a drone.

The Pentagon and its suppliers had been scrambling to field something, anything to defend against mass-produced, low-cost attack drones. They’ve rolled out radio frequency jammers, microwave weapons, an array of missiles, drones designed to kill other drones, even copies of the Iranian robots. None of them in isolation have been enough. On March 1, an Iranian drone killed six US service members and injured 30 others.

Pentagon and FAA officials went to White Sands less than a week later for a demo of an AeroVironment laser and assurances it could operate safely in a crowded airspace, according to The New York Times. (Lt. Gen Frank Lozano later said at a DC think tank event that the system had showed “a lot of recent promise and capability out at White Sands,” adding that the Army was “negotiating a contract with AeroVironment right now for the Enduring High Energy Laser system.”)

Two days after the White Sands display, President Donald Trump hyped the directed energy weapons’ capabilities.

“The laser technology that we have now is incredible,” he told reporters at his Doral, Florida club. “It’s coming out pretty soon, where literally lasers will do the work of—at a lot less cost—do the work of what the Patriots are doing.”

Now, the Army is expected to sign a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars with AeroVironment. According to the Army’s original request for information, that would be for up to 20 of the weapons. They’re supposed to be compact enough to fit inside in a four-by-seven foot container, or atop an all-terrain vehicle. And as Trump noted, they’re supposed to be powerful enough to knock out one-way attack drones# like the Shahed-136, the workhorse of Iran’s deadly unmanned arsenal. (Neither the Army nor AeroVironment agreed to comment for this story.)

But the truly novel development is that the Enduring High Energy Laser, or E-HEL, will be an operational “program of record,” military-speak for a formally approved piece of kit, officially inscribed in the Pentagon’s five-year budget. That's the military's sign to itself that this is for real, and a signal to contractors to ramp up production. “Program of record indicates a wider cultural acceptance of the new technology as a military capability,” says Craig Robin, who ran the directed energy portfolio for the Army’s Rapid Capabilities and Critical Technologies Office. It’s the first time the Army has ever done so with a laser weapon.

The basic physics of lasers have been well-understood for decades: Infuse an atom with enough energy and it goes into an “excited state,” in which the electrons orbit farther away from the nucleus. When the electrons come back down, they emit photons, and each one passing an excited atom triggers it to emit an identical photon: same frequency, same phase. Bounce that cascade between mirrors so it keeps building, and you get a powerful, coherent beam.

Which material, or “gain medium,” determines the light’s frequency; almost anything will work. “My own favorite is that a mixture of alcohol and quinine solution can actually be made to fluoresce, so you can actually do a laser martini,” Lewis says.

But just because you can make a laser martini doesn’t mean you should. Different gain media can produce different levels of power, at different levels of efficiency. That 747 used a mixture of chlorine, hydrogen peroxide, iodine, and other chemicals; it was powerful but toxic. The laser-equipped Humvee started out with a weapon that relied on a synthetic garnet crystal made of yttrium and aluminum; nontoxic but weak.

Eventually, most military laser-makers all turned to a single solution: “fiber lasers,” which rely on bundles of glass wires infused with rare-earth ions. They absorb energy more efficiently than the others, are better at releasing heat, and allow for an almost perfectly focused beam. Each individual fiber laser can’t produce that much power—just a few kilowatts—but they can be bundled together for weapons-grade work. And besides, the small drones these weapons would be used against don’t take that much power to take out.

“Exciting” the atoms inside those fibers got easier, thanks to advances in the semiconductor diodes (think LEDs, but with laser lights) that pump energy in, and get the chain reaction started. Advances in machine vision have helped the beams stay locked on target, while adaptive optics—mirrors that flex in real time to cancel out the shimmer of the atmosphere—keep them tightly focused. Put it all together, and you’ve got the makings of a laser weapon.

“The science for directed energy is largely done, and now we are in the engineering phase of it. So the engineering part of it makes it cheaper, smaller, and more proliferated,” Emil Michael, the under secretary of defense for research and engineering, told Congress in May.

It’s a song we’ve heard before. “The ray gun has finally become a reality,” The New York Times announced in 2008. A Popular Science cover story from 2006 showed illustrations of laser-firing stealth fighter jets and asked, “Can scientists end the era of bombs and bullets?”

I wrote that story. And the answer, then and now, is no.

Rain and fog stop lasers short. And lasers have to be fired at one target at a time, a few seconds per target. (Just look at this rather awkward demonstration of 60 Minutes host Leslie Stahl operating an AeroVironment weapon.) “So if you've got 1,000 drones coming in, you're not going to hit every single one,” says Scott Keeney, the CEO of nLight, a company that provides lasers to companies like AeroVironment and just won its own Pentagon contract, worth up to $627 million, to develop a laser that can take out a cruise missile. What’s more, lasers—especially the powerful ones he’s developing—keep going and going, even into orbit. “They just don’t stop,” Keeney says. Which means they could not only be a danger to aircraft but to satellites too.

In fact, the whole idea of swapping traditional munitions for lasers is “really dumb,” Lewis says. “The gun works fine. Why would you replace it with the laser? Use the laser in ways that you can't use the gun.”

Especially when the metaphorical gun, in this case, is a multimillion-dollar-per-shot interceptor system, and the target is a cheapo killer drone. Better to shine a beam of lethal light at it instead.

entries.title: The Best Gaming Mouse You Can Buy After Testing Dozens of Models
entries.summary: From wired to wireless to ultralight, we've tested dozens of gaming mice to find the best for work, your next MMO, and everything in between.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Picking a gaming mouse can be difficult. There are countless metrics to factor in and a nearly unlimited number of mice with unique approaches in defining what's best. Quite honestly, it’s a market rife with opportunities for analysis paralysis to take hold.

That’s why I take the time to test countless gaming mice—to tell you what works and what doesn’t. I can’t say precisely which mouse will work for you—that’s dependent not only on technical specs but on your preferences, needs, budget, and hand size—but hopefully I can provide some insights into the top options out there, what's the best for specific types of gamers, and why I’ve picked them.

Be sure to read our other peripheral buying guides for more, including the Best Ergonomic Mouse, Best Gaming Headsets, Best Mechanical Keyboards, and Best Hall Effect Keyboards.

Updated August 2026: I've added the Razer Viper V4 Pro and AngryMiao .97 Infinite as some of my favorite new mice. I've also moved other picks down and updated all pricing.

Other Good Gaming Mice to Consider

Corsair Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight for $130: When I first reviewed the new 36-gram Sabre, I was wowed by its weight but critical of its overly thin shell and flimsy construction. However, I accepted these as being a part of its innate nature as the lightest-possible mouse, and I’m incredibly glad that it exists. It’s a great option if you’re willing to sacrifice everything in the name of “simplifying and adding lightness,” as car designer Colin Chapman put it. But it's probably not the right choice if you want something that feels substantial or meaningful beyond that.

Corsair Sabre V2 Carbon Fiber and Magnesium for $170: While neither of these carry the same groundbreaking lightness of their predecessor (they both hover just below the 60-gram mark), they offer a much more refined design with premium materials and rigidity that’s unmatched by Corsair’s mainstream competitors. While they lag a bit behind in performance, they both feel fantastic to fling around a desk while providing a much more sturdy chassis that gives the impression they can withstand some serious use. Unless you really love the looks or science of carbon fiber, the less-expensive magnesium chassis is definitely the way to go in terms of both sturdiness and on-desk appeal.

Logitech Pro X Superlight 2 Dex for $160: This sculpted mouse predates the Deathadder V4 Pro by over a year and, because of this, the specs lag slightly behind it. However, the shape is just as comfortable, and the internals are still fantastic for anyone except the absolute most-discerning. The best part of this mouse is that, these days, it can easily be found on a significant discount. If you don’t want to shell out the extra cash for Razer’s latest model, or if you prefer Logitech’s software and styling, this is the mouse for you.

Corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE for $80: While MMO-focused mice aren’t finding themselves in the spotlight anymore (much like many of the MMOs that required numpads, and even numpads themselves, for that matter), there are still a few new models kicking around. The Scimitar is one of the most modern ones, adding adjustability to the classic numpad-on-the-side formula with a sliding rail to accommodate different grip styles and hand sizes. While this mouse obviously doesn’t compete with other models on this list in terms of technical specs or weight, it’s a really great mouse for the kinds of games that still necessitate having swathes of macros at your fingertips.

Steelseries Aerox 3 for $100: While it doesn’t have nearly the same weight or speed advantages as offerings from Razer and Logitech, the Aerox 3 is still a great mouse in its own special way. Weighing in at only 66 grams and being one of the only waterproof mice on this list (I literally ran it under a sink for a couple minutes to test this), this mouse is great for multi-user gaming computers, accident-prone individuals, and/or the poolside gaming setup of your dreams. Plus, built-in Bluetooth connectivity means you aren’t stuck with a dongle! However, 1000 Hz polling and 18,000 DPI do mean that, if you aren’t looking for something that’s more durable than average, you may be able to get a good bit more performance for a comparable price.

Logitech G203 for $27: Budget gaming mice often forgo a lot of the conveniences and performance you get out of nicer models, but the Logitech G203 never feels like it's lacking. The sensor has a lower maximum sensitivity than you'll get out of a more expensive offering—8,000 dots per inch—so if you need that top-end sensitivity, you'll want to look elsewhere, but it features six buttons, compatibility with Logitech’s G Hub software, and, most importantly, has RGB lighting. Those are all things you'd typically expect to pay more for.

Razer Viper V3 Pro for $100: The previous-gen Viper V3 Pro remains a solid choice, especially since it's selling for much less than the newer model. It remains an uncompromising mouse for lightweight, high-speed gaming performance. Despite being a couple of years old at this point, it still has competitive specs, the same great symmetrical shape, and some of the best-feeling buttons on the market. The battery lasts an incredibly long time (it’s rated for over 95 hours, and I didn’t need to charge it once during my testing). And with the included HyperPolling dongle, the mouse is capable of up to 8,000-Hz polling.

Sony Inzone Mouse-A for $148: Sony’s Inzone line is meant for a relatively upmarket audience, as evidenced by the price and build quality of both this mouse and its companion KBD-H75 keyboard. They are both incredibly well-made, with premium build quality and competitive specs. The Mouse-A is one of the lightest on this list, weighing only 48 grams. Despite this, it feels far more premium than other mice of comparable weight, using soft-touch plastics and feeling incredibly rigid during use. The mouse buttons feel good, with a subtle click, and the overall shape is simple and non-sculpted, comfortable for both left- and right-handed use (although it only has side buttons for right-handed users). This mouse has issues with wireless connectivity and battery life (between tests, I found it drained the entire battery life while disconnected), and I didn’t like the mouse wheel—there was a lot of space between each “bump” on the wheel, and I regularly found myself getting stuck between bumps when trying to scroll, resulting in a missed input. Like anything using a soft-touch coating, there is a concern that it will wear away and leave unsightly spots of exposed plastic with continuous use.

Great Mousepads

One of the cheapest things you can do to upgrade your PC gaming experience is to invest in a high-quality mousepad. If you’re a mouse-and-keyboard gamer, having the right surface for your trusty little rodent can be super helpful. Not only do you have a nice little area of your desk cordoned off for mouse use, but you also get a surface designed to be as friction-free and slick as possible—so you’ll be as quick as possible.

Harber London Professional Leather Desk Mat for $239: Despite more than a year of use, this Harber London leather desk mat still looks exquisite. The pebbled leather is supple and has a nice texture, but your mouse will glide over it effortlessly. It comes in three sizes and three colors.

SteelSeries QcK Mouse Pad for $11: SteelSeries’ QcK mousepad is one of my all-time favorites. The medium size is perfect for most desks, even small ones. It’s well-made and doesn’t fray easily—cheaper mousepads often fray at the edges, which ruins the aesthetic a good mousepad can lend to a workstation.

Grovemade Wool Felt Desk Pad for $70: This doesn't seem like your usual gaming accessory, because it's not. It's a wool felt pad from Portland, Oregon, company Grovemade, and it's large enough to fit a keyboard and a mouse with room to spare. It feels soft and plush under your wrists, and all of the gaming mice on this list just glide over its surface; it's like they're sliding on glass. It's a big surprise, honestly. Not to mention, a felt desk pad adds an air of sophistication and style to any desk, without making it seem too uptight. The color looks amazing under RGB lighting in a dark room. It's an easy and affordable way to inject some unique style into your work (and play) space.

What Makes a Good Gaming Mouse?

Here are a few features that really separate a gaming mouse from a regular came-with-my-PC kind of mouse:

Extra-sensitive optical sensors: Gaming mice should have more sensitive optical sensors that can detect smaller movements more quickly than a standard mouse.

More buttons: At a minimum, a good gaming mouse should have a clickable scroll wheel, a button for adjusting sensitivity, and two buttons where your thumb rests. Those extra thumb buttons can be lifesavers in competitive games.

Better buttons: They should also have higher-quality buttons, and more of them, than a standard office mouse. The left and right buttons should have individual switches inside, tensioned to register rapid clicks and reinforced to withstand more frequent clicks than a normal mouse. Top-of-the-line gaming mice often feature proprietary mechanical switches inside that give them a more tactile feel when you click.

Polling rate: For most games, the typical 1,000-Hz polling rate will be sufficient, but if you play a lot of fast-paced competitive games, where split-second actions can be crucial to victory, than you may get some benefit out of mice with faster polling rates.

Don't buy the DPI hype: Dots per inch (DPI) is a metric that describes a mouse’s overall sensitivity. A higher dpi means it can respond quicker, which is helpful in competitive online games. However, even if your mouse can go all the way up to, say, 20,000 dpi, most people (even in online games) keep their sensitivity around 1,000 to 1,600 dpi. More doesn’t necessarily mean better.

Your Palm Size and Grip Style Matters

A major aspect when shopping for a gaming mouse is size. Using a mouse that’s too small for your hand can cause strain on your hand and wrist, while a mouse that’s too large can feel unwieldy and be difficult to move precisely. It’s important to measure your hand and take into account the grip style you plan to use.

There are three primary mouse grips: Palm grip, claw grip, and fingertip grip. Palm grip is typically considered the most accurate but least agile, and it’s how most people use their mouse day-to-day. Your entire hand sits on the mouse, with your palm resting on the back half and your fingers laid along the mouse buttons. Claw grip is more agile, but will sacrifice some accuracy and stability. For this grip, you rest the bottom of your hand against the mouse while bending your fingers into a claw-like shape, leaving a significant amount of open air between your fingertips and the back of your hand. Fingertip grip has the least contact and allows for the most agility, but also sacrifices even more stability. With this grip, your hand will hover over the mouse, with your fingertips resting on the mouse buttons, and your thumb and pinky finger gripping the mouse from either side.

For a standard mouse used with a palm grip, the best way to determine the correct size is to measure the distance from the tip of your middle finger to the bottom of your palm, and compare those numbers to an online guide. Rocket Jump Ninja has a helpful tool for this, which also provides measurements of the recommended mice for cross-referencing. Alternatively, I’ve found it helpful to hold your hand in an arc as if you’re holding a mouse, and measure the distance from the bottom of your palm to your fingertips to get a measurement you can directly compare to mouse length. This method can also work for claw grip, but since the bottom of your palm will be resting directly on the mouse instead of sitting at the back, I find it better to err on the side of caution and pick a mouse that’s a few millimeters longer than you need.

Mouse sizing is dependent on the type of mouse you’re looking for: Whether chasing lightness or portability, there are quite a few short and small mice on the market. Compact or fingertip-grip mice like the Razer Basilisk Mobile or the G-Wolves Fenrir won’t fit the standard recommendations of mouse measurements. Instead, for a mouse like this (or any mouse you plan to use with a fingertip grip), I find it best to compare the mouse’s width to the distance between your thumb and your pinky finger (or your ring finger, depending on how you hold a mouse) in a comfortable gripping position. A mouse that’s too narrow can cause strain on your hand, while one that’s too wide can be difficult to properly grip and move.

entries.title: Purple Carrot Meal Kit Review: Tastier Than Meal Kits With Meat
entries.summary: I’m an omnivore. Purple Carrot’s vegan meal kit offers some of the best cooking I’ve seen from any meal kit, with or without meat.
entries.content:
Adventurous, delicious recipes with excellent culinary technique. Offers both meal kits and ready-to-eat premade meals. Doesn’t over-rely on soy.

TIRED

Recipes can be involved and time-consuming. Prepared meals are less fun than meal prep options.

The meals I made with vegan meal kit Purple Carrot include some of the best-tasting food I've made with any meal delivery service. This is no small statement. I'm an omnivore and longtime food critic who’s tested pretty much every meal delivery service in existence over the past two years.

And so when I say Purple Carrot offers good cooking, I'm not grading on a curve. Purple Carrot's pecan-topped, five-spice butternut squash dumplings I prepped this July were among the most extravagant meals I made for myself during that entire month. The prep was extensive, more than I'd usually attempt on any but a weekend evening, but the results were both healthful and a rival to excellent bistro fare.

Purple Carrot achieves this on its meal kit recipes while avoiding the pitfalls endemic to vegan fare—namely, an over-reliance on soy or cashew substitutes. Purple Carrot, thank God, loves a vegetable. It loves a fruit. And it loves an herb. While Purple doesn't offer a huge menu each week, and I was less enthralled by microwave meal options that resorted more often to hunks of seitan, the meal kit choices are both broad and appetizing.

Purple Carrot manages to deliver the classic promise of a meal kit—sweet relief from the same staid recipes I bore myself with when I'm out of ideas. It does so better than most meal kits that cater to meat-eaters. It was my colleague Molly Higgins' favorite plant-based meal kit of the dozen or so she tested last year. After testing five meals and a number of market add-ons this year, I rank it among my favorites overall.

Here's the rundown.

The Nuts and Bolts

Specs

Cost per meal

$13 to $15 per serving, plus $12 shipping per box. (Shipping free for orders above $120.)

Meal plan options

Two or four people; three or four meals a week for the classic meal kit. One to 10 meals a week for the ready-to-eat meal plan. Mix & match plans also available.

More than a third of meals are gluten-free. (But not certified as such for celiac, and prepared in a shared facility with wheat-containing products.)

Plant-based meals?

Vegan, vegan, all-vegan

Other dietary plans or restrictions

Individual meals marked as high-protein, high-fiber, low-calorie (<600), and low-sodium. Allergens clearly marked on each recipe.

Prep time

20 minutes to an hour for recipes; quick-prep meals as fast as 5 minutes

Purple Carrot is among the older meal delivery services in the United States, founded in 2014 in Massachusetts but later acquired by Japanese sustainable-focused food delivery company Oisix. Purple Carrot is indeed packaged more sustainably than most kits: cardboard insulation, recyclable paper containers for microwavable meals. One could also argue that plant-based food is sustainable by its nature. But there's still the usual battery of plastic baggies housing the various ingredients.

Though it's a subscription service, Purple Carrot's subscription is unusually flexible. Meals are priced individually, from $13 to $15 a serving, and can be mixed and matched among solo ready-to-heat meals and meal prep recipes for two or four. (Introductory plans lop half off your first week's order up to $100.) While you can cancel a week, each week does have a $65 minimum order—amounting to five or six servings.

Note also that Purple Carrot does not add a lot of fats and sugar to its meals, nor load up lots of carbs. Servings tend to range between 550 and 750 calories. That's a large lunch, and filling enough for medium appetites—but unlikely to stuff you if you're used to more heaping portions at dinner. In a trashmonster mood, I could hoover two servings and save my guilt for later.

Recipe ingredients are organized nicely into individual bags, and the foldout recipe cards are charmingly well designed and easy to save if you plan to replicate them in the future with or without Purple Carrot. The kits offer a mix of fresh produce and prepackaged ingredients that might include tofu, instant rice, or spice pouches.

Although produce isn’t guaranteed organic, most of the ingredients were (and of course, they were all vegan). The only ingredients you need to provide are salt, pepper, and cooking oil. Though note that at least one recipe—those excellent butternut squash dumplings—required a food processor, a rarity among meal kits loath to make such assumptions about anyone's home kitchen.

Good Cooking, Real Cooking

Purple Carrot's strength lies with the recipes and the freshness of the ingredients. Some sourcing is local where possible, according to Purple Carrot. And the produce I received did seem a step above most of the bigger meal kits. In my box, the poblanos were crisp, and the herbs were fragrant. In July, my corn came seasonably still on its cob, waiting to be sliced off into kernels. Avocado, a real worry for a delivery meal kit, was unbruised and ripe but not overripe.

This kind of freshness adds confidence. But it also adds prep. The butternut squash dumplings I prepared required that I throw squash and soy cream cheese into a food processor with herbs and spices, then individually fold the filling into a dozen dumpling wrappers, before then frying up the dumplings and toasting a sesame-pecan topper. In the meantime, I'll be slicing up apples for a little citrus-y salad.

That recipe is advertised at just under an hour: It will take every bit of it. It's also worth it—a nice balance of crisp and soft, comforting and brightly acidic.

But most recipes sport advertised prep times closer to 30 minutes. Other recipes, like rajas avocado tacos with corn straight off the cob, aren't much harder to prep than merely slicing the vegetables. Beyond this, the recipe called for a short turn in the broiler and oven for both veggies and tortillas. I'll admit, I didn't want to heat the oven on a hot summer day, and so I instead griddled the ingredients on a broad All-Clad stainless steel pan, and it was both faster and delicious. The meal took maybe 20 minutes to prep, even less than advertised.

As a taco topper, the recipe also called for drizzling lime and salt onto sliced avocado—a bit like guacamole without the mush. This was kinda terrific. But the biggest factor in the recipe's deliciousness was probably the quality of the thick corn tortillas: They were every bit as masa-forward as the local packaged tortilla brand I favor in my own kitchen, which usually arrives within days of being made. For a meal kit, a tortilla like this is a rare offering.

A peanut-studded chili tofu dish, meanwhile, carried vague whiffs of Indonesia without making false claims: complex, savory, lightly spicy, lightly sweet. Textures were a nice little school in contrasts among the peanuts, the fried-hard exterior of the tofu, and the soft interior of each cube. It's the sort of recipe that feels easy to adapt into variations later.

The Caveats

As mentioned, Purple Carrot offers some of the best cooking I've seen from meal subscription services, and some of the more sophisticated flavors. But at times, this also requires a bit of experience in the kitchen. Directions are clear and easy to follow. But handholds are few.

If there's a consistent gripe, it's that the recipes are perhaps too concise: Preparation steps are often hidden in the ingredients list. When the recipe calls for “parsley, leaves and tender stems minced (divided),” what they actually mean is that you should separate and mince the parsley leaves and stems. Beginning chefs may have a hard time reading between the lines and thus doing appropriate prep in advance—leading to a scramble during later cooking steps.

I found the recipe cook times mostly honest, a rarity among meal kits. But in part, that's because I found myself compressing timeframes on recipes by reading ahead and doing a little planning, often performing multiple items simultaneously. For cooks less prone to multitasking, cook times might end up significantly longer than advertised. (This said, I actually came in under time on two recipes.)

But while I loved the recipes, I had less use for the microwavable meals I tried, whether a Korean-fried “chicken” with rice or a spaghetti with soy meatballs. In part, this is because I'm not much of a fan of soy as a substitute for meat to begin with. But it was also unclear that the microwave did its texture any favors.

The biggest sell for the meals I tried was that each was a substantial source of protein—more than 40 grams in each meal. For vegans, or those watching saturated fats, the convenient access to high-protein meals without the meat might be advertisement enough. Neither reheatable meal was better, nor worse, than B-minus.

But it's the prepped meals that I ended up loving, and that I'll both recommend and likely return to. Purple Carrot shows mastery across a broad palette of worldwide flavors and ingredients, without the compromises that too often come with wide-ranging recipes. Speaking as a man who loves a steak but needs to watch his cholesterol, I'd also happily find myself ordering Purple Carrot instead.

entries.title: The Best Cordless Vacuums (2026): My Brand-New Top Pick
entries.summary: Clean your house without the constraint of a power cord, thanks to these stick vacuums.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

It may sound hyperbolic to claim the best cordless vacuums can improve your life. But they do hold that power. In addition to providing you the freedom you didn't know you needed, they also leave your home clean and tidy in a matter of minutes with no cord unraveling or heavy vacuum dragging required. These machines are especially handy for me, as I live in a three-story home. Even the prospect of lugging a classic upright vacuum up and down the stairs leaves me unlikely to do the chore. And I can never seem to remember to take my robot vacuum to different floors to clean the whole house. A stick vacuum, though? Because the form is light and mobile, these vacuums are a breeze to bring to every level and use on my two sets of stairs—and I only expend a tiny bit of sweat in the process.

After testing nearly two dozen stick vacuums—including hard-floor–only models, powerful Dysons, and more—these are the best cordless vacuums I've tried. My new favorite is the Shark PowerDetect Speed Cordless Stick Vacuum ($430), which not only has impressive power but also bends to make vacuuming under furniture and low surfaces easier. It also has the Clean & Empty version ($500), which features a self-emptying base station. If you've got room to splurge, you can upgrade to the Dyson Gen5Detect ($800) for the best power I've seen in a cordless vacuum.

Looking for more cleaning gadgets? Don't miss our guides to the Best Dyson Vacuums, Best Robot Vacuums, Best Vacuums for Pet Hair, and Best Handheld Vacuums. For extra intel about vacuums and how often to use them, check out our guides to How Often You Should Vacuum and How Long Vacuums Really Last.

Updated July 2026: I’ve added the Shark PowerDetect Speed, the Dyson Gen5Detect, and the Dyson V10 Konical as picks. I've also added testing details on the Dyson V16 Piston Animal, Dyson V8 Cyclone, and Levoit Aero Cordless.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Jump to Section

Honorable Mentions

Bissell's PowerClean FurFinder for $160: This is a great stick vacuum, and it was my previous top pick. It does an all-around good job on all kinds of flooring, comes with a nice range of accessories, and has the FurFinder tool to help with pet hair. It's still a great vacuum, especially if you have pets, but unless you're using the FurFinder tool frequently, you can get the slightly cheaper regular Bissell PowerClean for a similar experience.

Dyson PencilVac Fluffycones for $600: This vacuum is impressively lightweight and easy to use, and I really like it for quick daily cleans. The Dyson PencilVac manages to fit its extra-small motor and dustbin into the handlebar, so this vacuum is free of the bulky top you'll find on just about every other cordless vacuum. The downside is that it has a low suction-power level of 50 air watts and only works on hard floors. It has started clogging frequently for me, too, after a few months of use. It works well for quick sweeps, and I like the lightweight design for anyone with strength or mobility concerns, but it's a hefty price tag for a limited version of a cordless vacuum.

Dyson V15 Detect for $850: This is another good Dyson vacuum, but while it has more powerful suction (240 AW) than Dyson's newer, cheaper models, it didn't do better in side-by-side tests against the V10 Konical. It is nice that the V15 vacuum comes with the Fluffy Optic head for hard floors, has a Submarine variant for mopping, and is still a solid all-around performer. I'd snag it on sale for the extra head, but I wouldn't buy it at full price.

Dyson V16 Piston Animal for $850: This is Dyson's new top-of-the-line vacuum. It packs the highest suction power I've seen on a Dyson cordless vacuum—315 air watts—and it does a good job overall with vacuuming several types of floors thanks to the All Floor Cones Sense head that's made for both hard floors and carpets. There's also the Fluffy Optic head included for hard floors, and you can upgrade to the Submarine version ($1,100) to make it double as a wet mop. Even so, I found the Gen5Detect to work just as well, if not slightly better in some tests. So unless you want to add on the mop (or the forthcoming self-emptying base station that Dyson has coming out), you'll be just as happy spending a little less on the Gen5Detect. If you spot it on sale, though, it's worth grabbing over a full-price Gen5Detect.

Levoit Aero Cordless Vacuum for $300: This stick vac comes with a self-emptying charging station, freeing you from the responsibility of manually emptying the vacuum. There's a five-stage HEPA filtration system that claims to capture 99.97 percent of particles (as small as 0.3 microns), making it ideal for people who want to reduce pet allergens around their home. This vacuum also doubles as a hand vacuum for easier, lighter-weight cleaning and comes with a slew of handy attachments for those hard-to-reach places, including crevice and combination tools, a mini motorized brush, and an extension hose for longer reach. It works excellently on both high- and low-pile carpets, pulling up microscopic dust and dirt better than other vacuums I’ve tested. My main gripe is that it isn't nearly as effective on hardwood floors. —Molly Higgins

Shark PowerDetect Cordless Vacuum for $330: Shark's PowerDetect is a fantastic vacuum. It was my previous top pick and is still an excellent buy, especially if you spot it on sale, or if you want a slightly longer battery life than the PowerDetect Speed I recommend above. There are three cleaning modes, lights on both the front and back of the vacuum head to spot debris, and detection technology to sense when you're cleaning edges or when a specific area is dirtier than other spots. You’ll also get 70 minutes of run time, a HEPA filter, and the central stick can even bend so you can vacuum under furniture without crouching on the ground. It comes with two attachments, and you can upgrade to a model with a self-emptying docking station ($550).

Other Vacuums I’ve Tested

Bissell IconPet Turbo Edge for $266: Bissell's OG stick vacuum is a popular model that's been around for a while. It does a good job at picking up hair and cat litter, and it easily turns into a handheld vac. The battery life is also nice, but former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano wasn't impressed by its lacking Cheerios-gathering skills, and the machine also can't stand up on its own.

Bosch Unlimited 10 Cordless Stick Vacuum for $529: This vacuum has six cleaning modes, can bend in the middle, and its motor has a long warranty. When I recently retested it, it was better at sucking up cat litter on hard floors (using its main cleaner head) than Dyson's All Floor Cones head and Shark's PowerDetect Speed vacuum. Overall, it performed similarly to some Dyson vacuums, but didn't outpace Shark, which has a better price point.

Black & Decker Powerseries Extreme Max for $199: A great stick vacuum for a lower-end price, the Black & Decker Powerseries Extreme Max stands up on its own, has three power levels you can easily control from the handle, and handles well on the different surfaces in my home. I liked this vacuum a lot, but it wasn't as stable as the Bissell above, and the handle felt a little plasticky compared to it and other vacuums I tested. It did have a larger-capacity dustbin, though.

Dirt Devil Power Swerve Pet Cordless Stick Vacuum for $89: I previously recommended this as a budget pick. It's a good vacuum for the money, but the battery life and build quality were questionable.

Dyson V8 Cyclone for $400: I really wanted to like this new generation of the popular V8 vacuum, but if you're going to choose one of Dyson's new, more affordable vacuums, go with the V10 Konical. It outperformed the V8 in every test I ran and only costs $100 more. They both have 150 air watts of power, but the V10 has the new All Floor Cones head and a built-in light to help you spot debris on hard floors.

Dyson V12 Detect for $650: The V12 Detect has the same power level (150 air watts) as the newer V8 and V10, both of which are cheaper than the V12, so I'd pick those over this older model.

Eufy Robot Vacuum 3-in-1 E20 for $440: WIRED reviewer Adrienne So was stoked to try Eufy's E20, which is a stick vacuum, handheld vacuum, and robot vacuum all in one. It's a handy, well-designed device, but it's only good for light cleaning.

Eureka Stylus Elite for $190: This is a good stick vacuum with a self-emptying bin at a reasonable price. It cleaned up a litter mat especially well, and there are specific settings for carpet and hardwood. However, to suck up larger pieces like Cheerios, I had to lift the vacuum and place it directly on top of the cereal pieces.

Levoit LVAC-300 for $230: This is a well-rounded stick vacuum has a good price point (and is often on sale). It has an hour of battery life, HEPA filtration, comes with a couple of accessories, and has similar specs to our favorite Dyson vacuum. The light 6.6-pound weight also made cleaning the three sets of stairs in WIRED reviewer Luke Larson's home fairly easy. While it can stand on its own, beware that it tips over easily.

Ryobi 18V One+ HP Advanced Stick Vacuum Kit for $399: This is our runner-up cordless vacuum pick for the best pet-hair vacuums. It has powerful suction, cyclonic filtration, a brushless motor, an easily removable roller bar, and lights on the vacuum head to better see pet hair and dander.

Tineco Pure One Station 5 for $299: I love that this vacuum has a self-emptying base station. It's a solid vacuum overall, but my favorite part is the docking station. You don't need to choose Tineco to enjoy that feature, though; Shark has a few models with self-emptying stations, and Dyson has one due out this year.

Worx 20V Cordless Stick Vacuum for $238: This is a fine vacuum, but the dustbin was more difficult to clean out than those of other models I tested.

FAQs

What's a Cordless Vacuum?

Cordless vacuums, also known as stick vacuums, are exactly what their name suggests: They don't need a cord to work. Instead, they have a battery you need to charge. Their typical design features a battery and motor at the top, with a long, thin, stick-like body connecting that to the head of the vacuum. They're much lighter than an upright vacuum and have become popular since they're much easier to store and move around the house. As someone who lives in a three-story home, stick models are my favorite type of vacuum, thanks to their comparatively lightweight nature and portability. Stick vacuums can also usually have the stick portion removed to transform into a handheld vacuum, though they're much heavier than a true handheld vacuum (but the battery life is much better).

How Long Do Cordless Vacuums Last?

Overall, vacuums tend to last around five years, but that depends on the frequency with which you vacuum and the vacuum's build quality. Some cheaper stick vacuums might last only about a year or two, though, according to Eufy, so it's worth investing in a good-quality stick vacuum. For information on the signs your vacuum may need replacing, check out our guide to how long vacuums can last. If you're curious whether you're vacuuming enough, check out our guide to how often you should vacuum.

How Does WIRED Test Cordless Vacuums?

The best way to test a vacuum is to use it like you usually would. So, for a few months, we lived with these cordless vacuums, using them to handle day-to-day messes along with weekly deep cleans on hardwood floors, area rugs, and carpets. We charged them, asked our partners to use them, and even took some to a retail store to clean up antique furniture.

We also performed head-to-head testing, comparing how each model picked up piles of Cheerios and cat litter, noting whether they blew debris around or needed several passes to clean a certain spot. We also took heaps of already matted dust and dirt from inside the vacuum bins to see how easily the vacuums could suck them back up in their thickened state.

entries.title: Is This Poker Player Bluffing? The AI Thinks So
entries.summary: ESPN unveiled an “AI tells detection” tool during broadcasts of the 2026 World Series of Poker. Is it a neat computer-powered party trick, or a real threat to poker’s future?
entries.content:
For serious poker players, the ability to sniff out the “tells” that expose an opponent’s intentions is nearly as important to winning as the cards themselves.

Many gamblers have made careers out of their ability to decipher the meaning of everything other players do at the table—their conscious movements, their body language, and their subconscious tics, all of which might reveal their strategy—as a method of gaining an edge in this game of incomplete information.

It’s understandable, then, that ESPN’s use of a new “AI tells detection” tool during the 2026 World Series of Poker Main Event broadcast stoked some serious debate within the poker community.

The tool began appearing periodically during the first few days of the tournament’s live broadcast in early July. A text overlay displayed various live metrics on a player’s movements, plus a “hand strength model” chart breaking down different possibilities of the type of hand a player might be holding. The tool looks slick, but a viewer might naturally wonder how accurate its data is, or how the AI came to know the players’ tics and gestures well enough to venture such a guess.

Is the tool just a neat party trick—or a silly one, depending on your sensibilities? Or is it an attempt to haphazardly stuff AI into the inherently human pursuit of poker, threatening the game’s soul and future?

Do Tell

Hundreds of pros on the poker circuit specialize in spotting tells. This new tool, designed by an AI engineer for the US Air Force named Luke Geel, purports to digitize that process. It’s watched every hand captured on camera in the 2026 WSOP Main Event to build a tells database on various players.

The system gathers inputs on the players ranging from eye movements and the rate at which they blink, to the players’ posture, chip handling movements, “hand fidget” metrics, and more. It analyzes that data and the outcomes of each hand to predict the likelihood of which general hand type a player might have: A strong made hand, a drawing hand, a bluff, and so on.

The poker experts I spoke to are skeptical about the tool’s effectiveness—especially since it was trained on such a small amount of data. The 2026 edition of the WSOP Main Event tournament drew over 9,000 entries, but the vast majority of those players never spent time at one of three tables that were being recorded by cameras. (The same camera feeds used for the broadcast were also used to train the AI tool). Even those who did sit at those tables weren’t there long enough for the system to build a robust dataset that covers the vast range of situations possible in poker.

“The streams are varied enough that you don't get the same players too frequently,” says Michael Gagliano, a 17-year poker professional who made the Main Event final table this year and is playing for the $10 million top prize this week.

Gagliano, who started the final in eighth chip position, says he went back through every second of ESPN’s live streams during the two-and-a-half-week break after the final table was reached in mid-July, combing for any tells or info he could pick up on his remaining opponents. But that lack of screen time for any one player limited his ability to spot the tells, even for players who made it all the way to the final table and spent lots of time on camera.

“I don't know how much actual information I'm going to be able to act on from what I saw,” he says.

Any AI looking at the footage would face the same issue, even for a tournament as long as the Main Event.

More Than Just Cookies

Tell detection is nuanced work, and pros are dubious that a camera-based AI tool can effectively do it better than a human.

Most nonplayers’ exposure to the importance of poker tells comes from the penultimate scene in the 1998 film Rounders. Matt Damon’s character, Mike McDermott, folds a monster hand to John Malkovich’s Teddy KGB after recognizing that the gangster has him beat—and McDermott discovers this after spotting a tell based on KGB’s habit of eating Oreos at the table. It’s arguably the most memorable poker scene in movie history because it perfectly expresses the battle of wits that underlies every poker game, even though in reality it’s quite reductive.

“To reference the Rounders Oreo cookie tell, it’s a little more abstract than that,” says Shaun Deeb, a two-time winner of the WSOP Player of the Year award and one of the most recognizable players in the game. (Deeb also made a deep run in the 2026 Main Event, finishing 15th.)

“Physical tells are so much more expansive than I think the public realizes,” Deeb says. “There are leg tells, checking tells, verbal tells, breathing tells, pulse tells. There's an insane amount of tells available, and most of those can't be picked up by a camera.”

An AI can track visual and audio patterns, but it can’t deduce intention; the former is only so valuable without the latter. Even if the tool was hypothetically perfect at determining when a player was projecting confidence or weakness, that alone isn’t a road map to deciphering their actual hand.

“How strong is two pair to one player versus another player?” says Gagliano. “Maybe someone is extra confident with a hand that’s actually weak for the situation, but for some reason they think they have the best hand, so they’re really confident.

“Maybe if I was playing a casual tournament, I would think my two pair is extremely strong. But in the Main Event I'm still a little nervous, because it's a high-stakes situation. So maybe my body language is referencing the situation rather than the hand strength.”

For a broadcast entertainment tool, those flaws aren’t necessarily a deal-breaker. No one is expecting some all-knowing oracle—Geel, the tool’s creator, least of all. He’s transparent about the fact that a larger sample of hands would be better for his tool, telling WIRED via email that he’s run some blind tests on other poker competitions with mixed results.

Maybe the feature adds value for some ESPN viewers, though players like Deeb are skeptical even of that. “I think they randomly found something to try to make it like another sport, and I just think it was swing-and-a-miss,” Deeb says.

While viewers saw the tool in action during portions of the tournament broadcast in July, a representative from Omaha Productions, a company licensed by ESPN for WSOP and other sports coverage, said in a text message that the tool would not be used for the final table. The representative declined to provide any reasoning for that decision.

Watching the Detectives

As AI continues to improve, even skeptics concede it’s possible tools like these evolve rapidly and will likely be applied for financial gain. Within poker’s “high-roller” tournament scene, where the buy-ins frequently reach six figures, a small pool of mostly recognizable professionals play each other in events that are often broadcast. It’s possible that hundreds or even thousands of hours of footage exist of these top players, many of whom play dozens of such events every year. It’s already common for poker players to study streamed and broadcast footage to gather info on their regular opponents. Could improved AI optimize that very human process?

Deeb, for one, isn’t worried. As a top pro, he’s frequently been hired to coach players as they make deep runs in the Main Event; he says that process has often included bringing in a hand-picked live tells specialist to observe both opponents and the client themselves (to see if they have any glaring tendencies that should be corrected). A close friend of Deeb’s was watching the streams during his run this year as well, doing the same thing on his behalf.

While he’ll use recorded footage if it’s the only option available, Deeb says the filmed route isn’t optimal.

“The teams I hired, we always had a spot for the person spotting the tells to be watching the player in person,” he says. “We thought it was much better than what you get on TV.”

Tools like the one ESPN is using are naturally not allowed at any live poker table. Some tournaments or high-stakes cash games lock things down even further, limiting or outright banning any electronic devices on the table’s surface that would enable cheating. Deeb predicts Meta smart glasses and similar devices will be outlawed before long for similar reasons. Even if a player has an AI they believe has given them a perfect list of their opponents’ tells, they still have to spot the tells themselves when they’re at the table—all while avoiding giving away any information of their own.

And as long as that remains the case, Deeb isn’t losing sleep over an AI outperforming him or other top pros, no matter how advanced it gets.

“I would take my team versus the AI,” he says. “And make a bet on it.”

entries.title: How One Startup Built a (Mostly) China-Free Robot
entries.summary: Ati Robotics assembles its robots in India and uses just a few Chinese parts—a strategy that could pay off as the Trump administration cracks down on Chinese humanoids.
entries.content:
Last week, US regulators banned a wide variety of Chinese-made robots from being imported to the United States because of concerns about national security. Saurabh Chandra was ready to seize the moment. His company, Ati Robotics, assembles its robots in India, and Chandra believes they use fewer Chinese parts than almost any other robotics company in the US.

Investment in robotics startups hit record highs this year, both in the number of deals and dollars invested, according to PitchBook, which tracks venture capital flows. But many of those companies primarily develop software, and they largely still rely on Chinese suppliers for their hardware.

The Federal Communications Commission’s decision to ban new models of human-like robots, known as humanoids, and other advanced devices from China could hamper the growth of many smaller robotics firms in the US. But some businesses could benefit, including Ati.

The startup was founded in 2017 to develop motors for self-driving cars. Years later, it zeroed in on making its own robots, including tuggers and pallet movers that cart tons of materials throughout big facilities. Ati developed its own hardware, believing that it would lead to better functionality, a bet that Chandra says many of his advisers cautioned against but one that wound up naturally limiting reliance on China.

It has begun to pay off. Ati has several hundred robots currently in operation at warehouses and factories and more than 50 customers in total, Chandra says. Ati’s first humanoid, which moves heavy bins around, will go into service later this year.

Chandra spoke with WIRED last week about how Ati Robotics steered clear of China, while building robots he argues can still compete with the industry’s best on price and performance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

WIRED: Developing hardware is expensive. How were you able to financially sustain doing that?

Saurabh Chandra: R&D is in Bangalore, which helps with our labor costs. Bangalore was undergoing this electric vehicle revolution in the two-wheeler, three-wheeler category in India. And it turns out that the kind of vehicles we were making for the robotics industry happened to have a similar power profile and characteristic as the two-wheeler and three-wheelers being made in the EV industry.

We tried to leverage the components and supply chain being developed for those vehicles. Typically, automotive parts are very reliable and are produced in large volumes, hence they are very good and cost-efficient. Though we had to do engineering with some of those vendors to make the parts work in a robot. But once we did, we had a great win.

One of your robot models is China-free, right, but not the others?

They have different levels of what I might call “supply chain resiliency.” Two of our best-selling models—our 10,000-pound tugger and the pallet mover—use very few parts from China. They're tugging trolleys—you may be taking raw material from stores to the factory line or from one process point to another.

But even with the humanoid that we have, the full arm is done here in Bangalore. The actuator is also done here, but we do get the harmonic drive from China, for example, and the frameless motor, at least for now.

The battery cells come from China. But we could, for example, get the cells from South Korea or Japan tomorrow. So those are passive components. There are some components that do come from China when we go deeper. We use induction motors, so even the magnet in the motor is not coming from China. That’s a very different choice from many of the people who are doing robots.

Which of your robots uses the fewest parts from China?

The 10,000-pound tugger. It's really China-free actually. And even the pallet mover has maybe less than 5 percent Chinese parts.

Which part of the tugger do you still need from China?

Just the cells in the battery. In the pallet mover, we use one very good solid-state lidar sensor, which we don't have an option from outside China. But in the tugger, we use Ouster, which is a US-based lidar sensor.

Did you have to make some trade-offs?

Yeah, we used induction motors, which are slightly less efficient than, say, Chinese-made brushless motors, which have magnets in them. But you can trade off a bit of efficiency for a bit more battery.

How do you market your robots? Is your supply chain part of the appeal?

That's not been a big part of our marketing, to be honest, but we do let customers know. We have not seen this being a very explicit part of their buying criteria. But many customers have definitely told us that it influences their decisions.

How do you plan to make your new humanoid robot less reliant on parts from China?

It's very early. We don't try to optimize the supply chain from the get-go. The gears come from China right now, but those gears are also manufactured in Germany, Taiwan, and Japan. So they'll be a little more expensive than the ones we get from China, but alternatives are available.

With this new ban in place, do you think it's going to be easy for US companies to find alternative suppliers?

The regulation is not saying that you cannot use any part from China. But quite a few people will be impacted in my opinion. Absolutely. Most of these robots have been invented in the US. It's a bit of a tragedy that we are not making them in the US. Maybe more people will be encouraged to make them locally, which is not a bad thing.

Where is your humanoid ultimately assembled?

Currently, we manufacture all of these robots in Bangalore, but we are setting up a facility in Madison Heights near Detroit, Michigan, where we will eventually assemble them in the future.

How are people in the robotics industry reacting to the new ban?

Everyone’s in denial. Absolutely. It'll get real. A couple of months ago, I had met people at a conference, and they were actively trying to lobby in Washington, DC, to prevent something like this from happening, but I don't think they succeeded.

Who do you think will ultimately benefit from the new ban?

Everybody who is trying to make robots outside of China, including robotics companies in the US and Europe. We are an accidental beneficiary. Tesla’s Optimus is obviously a clear beneficiary. Figure (a robotics startup) manufactures in the US. I hope more people get inspired. It's not like what we are doing is magic.

entries.title: ‘Everyone Is Doing It’: The Truth About AI in Hollywood
entries.summary: Puck’s Matthew Belloni says AI has quietly become part of everyday filmmaking. The battle now isn’t whether Hollywood will use the technology—it’s who controls what’ll come next.
entries.content:
If you want a clear understanding of how AI is affecting Hollywood … good luck.

Some of the industry loathes the technology, with screenwriters, directors, and actors alike vowing never to use AI in their work—or collaborate with those who do. Others are much more open to the potential for AI to act as everything from creative partner to cost-cutting engine. And a rare few, Ben Affleck included, are already making millions by capitalizing on AI’s nascent potential to (they argue) streamline and improve the filmmaking process.

At WIRED, we’re constantly doing our best to document AI’s transformational effects on the entertainment business, for better and for worse. (If you haven’t read Ruth Fowler’s recent essay for us, on going from a screenwriter to an underemployed LLM trainer, I highly recommend it.) But in an effort to get the most nuanced possible view, I wanted to talk to someone who knows the industry and its players inside and out.

Matt Belloni, a founding partner at Puck, has covered Hollywood for decades. He writes a scoopy newsletter (What I’m Hearing …) and hosts a scoopy podcast (The Town) that frequently focus on AI and Big Tech as both become increasingly dominant forces across entertainment. Belloni also happens to be a former lawyer, making him the ideal person to ask about the ongoing, and highly consequential, debates over AI and copyright, IP, and celebrity likeness.

Belloni was generous enough to give me an hour of his time, and we managed to cover all the bases—from whether Hollywood types side-eyed Ben Affleck after he sold an AI startup to Netflix for $587 million, to just how much control Big Tech companies now wield over the entertainment industry. You can read our conversation above or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Matt, I have to start with the obvious, which is artificial intelligence. You've been on top of AI in Hollywood for a very long time, and you've said multiple times that, quote, “everyone is doing it,” meaning everyone [in the industry] is using AI. What exactly do you mean by that?

MATTHEW BELLONI: Well, there's two types of AI, as you know. There's generative AI, which is content creation and things like that, and then there's what I refer to as the corporate AI, like streamlining processes and better search results. Obviously, on the second one, everyone is using it.

I'm not going to name a name, but I heard a very interesting story about a very prominent showrunner who went into the writer's room and basically castigated her writing team for not using ChatGPT to help with the process.

To help with the creative process? Or the admin and bookkeeping?

The creative process. Here's a scenario, suggest some jokes. Here's this, this, this. It doesn't mean they use them. You could do the same thing with Google. It's just better, and people are using it. I know, I've talked to screenwriters who use it to suggest scenarios or to give a description of the inside of a building where they want a scenario to play out, or things that to me seem like part of the process.

You may not know this, but the Writers Guild is actually OK with that. As long as there is a credited writer on every script and that this process doesn't impact jobs, they're OK with the use of this technology.

That's one side. Then the other side is generative and how this is making content. There it's a little murkier, because there are a lot of studios that are purporting to create AI-generated movies, shorts, TV pilots. I've seen a lot of them. They're not great. They're better in animation, and I think this is where we're going to see the disruption first, but you can always kinda tell, and that's the problem when you're trying to relate to people. I can't wait to see what Elon's historically accurate version of The Odyssey looks like.

I mean, it's obviously going to be spectacular. I'm sure he's hard at work on it. He's probably been staying up all night, all week.

First of all, historically accurate is hilarious for a work of fiction. But it just means it's going to be all white people. And the funny thing is, if he tries to use or to scrape the actual version of [Christopher Nolan’s] The Odyssey—I don't know if you saw the headlines, a full version of The Odyssey leaked on X last weekend, and before Universal could send a takedown, it was viewed like a million times …

I actually had not seen that.

So who knows whether Grok got its hands on the actual Odyssey to train for Elon’s fake Odyssey, but whatever.

On the generative AI front, I think where we’re seeing the biggest innovation/disruption is in the animation world, where visually scenes can be completed and storyboards done without the use of artists. You can extrapolate things. Doesn't mean it's the finished product, but even Netflix, on their earnings call this past month, said that 300 shows use generative AI.

I saw that. And they're talking about that relatively loudly and freely. I'm wondering where the stigma is right now. Are there members of Hollywood—actors, directors, screenwriters—who are calling out AI publicly while using it privately? How much of this is still happening behind closed doors in secretive circumstances?

Well, obviously I don't know what everybody does behind closed doors, but I know what people I talk to say to me. I do know that there is still a taint on using it.

A perfect example is Amazon. They did a whole media day where they brought in press and they have this whole AI generative studio that is being run by Albert Chang, one of their executives, and they announced a bunch of shows, including some animation shows, and there were real creators on these shows.

Almost immediately, the backlash that one of the creators got online was so crazy—I don't say crazy meaning bad, I mean crazy like loud—that he stepped down. That's a tangible impact of AI shaming, so to speak, and that is real.

You know, maybe that'll change. Netflix got a lot of leeway on this, because what did they do? They bought Ben Affleck's AI company. They paid almost 600 …

$587 million. And I barely knew he had an AI company until he sold it.

I asked the question, “Was this a $600 million press release?” Because Netflix wants to get into AI. They know that Ben is someone who has a ton of credibility and cachet as a movie star, an Oscar winner, a filmmaker, and having him attached to this company buys them a lot of leeway and allows them to do things that maybe others would bristle at, but it's Ben’s company. He's vouching for it.

And if you look at what that product actually does, it takes the footage that you have shot, and it makes it available for generative AI, essentially.

So it prevents you from having to do a costly reshoot if all you need is some coverage of something. It allows you to extend the periphery of a scene or get a circle shot when you didn't get it in camera. It’s much more of a tool for filmmakers—or at least this is how they've presented it—than something that is replacing [them], because the big fear in Hollywood is that this technology will replace [people].

What was the talk of the town, so to speak, when Ben made that deal? Did people scratch their heads? Did they look at him differently than they had the day before?

I honestly don't think so. There are a number of filmmakers that are doing this, and doing it the so-called right way. Darren Aronofsky is one of them—and Ben, I think because of his credibility and because he's able to articulate very clearly what he's actually doing and what he's not doing.

Because of that, I think that it went over OK. I think the biggest reaction I heard was like, "Holy cow, $600 million?"

That's a lot of money.

He's gonna make more money on that than he's made on any of his movies put together.

Well, he's had some, I don't know, expensive divorces.

I know. The question is, did he launch it when he was married to JLo? I imagine their prenups probably contemplate their separate property.

I think they had a very expensive house they were trying to offload at one point. I'm a big entertainment gossip reader.

There have been a bunch of deals between tech firms and Hollywood. There was the $75 million investment from Google DeepMind into A24, which pissed a lot of fans off. You had Lionsgate taking a stake in Runway, which is a big name in AI-generated video.

Why is this happening? Is it that the technology is ready? Is it that Hollywood is more receptive to this idea that, potentially, the technology can really have an impact on the industry?

I think there's a couple things. First of all, the technology is better, and it is applicable, and there's this fear in the C-suites of the entertainment companies of being left behind. If you talk to people at the studios, one of the biggest problems they face is the cost of movies. The cost of movies keeps going up, whereas the box office is not necessarily covering that.

If you look at the animation space, Pixar is a perfect example. Pixar originals, they can't make them for less than $200 million. I mean, they can, but it's very difficult to make them. They're made in California with a California workforce. They have their own special process that is very labor-intensive, and they haven't used AI to the extent that they maybe could.

If we are looking at a new landscape where movies just aren't going to gross as much as they did, you have to look at bringing the cost down.

And the guilds aren't bringing the cost of labor down. The unions are not willing to do that. So where does it come from? It comes from non-unionized labor that is, for the most part, the below-the-line people and the technology.

That makes me think of Christopher Nolan and The Odyssey. It had a huge cast, it was made all over the world. It's making crazy money. And Chris Nolan, who I believe still professes to not having a phone, not surprisingly has also been critical of AI while also being open to its uses, right?

He's kind of a fence-sitter. But he has also pointed out that younger generations have rejected a lot of quote-unquote slop, right? They're looking for authenticity. That said, are the Chris Nolans of the world going to continue to be even more the exception to the rule?

He is a one of one at this point, where he came into this situation with all the credibility and clout in the world, having won the Oscar for Oppenheimer and having made a billion dollars off that movie. The Odyssey, if it is made at all by another filmmaker, it's made at a much lower cost, not $250, almost $300 million. You don't get to have all those stars in it. You just don't get to do it.

But what I would argue to the studios is that is exactly why it broke through, is that it smells different. If you look at the trailer, if you look at everything around it, it smells authored, and the audience can tell when something is authored.

In a world where you can create all the visual effects you want, there's something about seeing The Odyssey and knowing, because they are very good at marketing this, that this is the vision of one guy who you trust and who is gonna show you something real. And I say real in the sense that movies are increasingly going to be split into movies that are filmed with real people and real scenarios and then those that are just either generative AI in practice or generative AI from the get-go.

There's going to be a split between things that we find authentic and those that we just kind of passively enjoy.

Just sort of consume, for lack of a better term.

That's where social media is going, and the more social video goes that direction, I think the bigger the market opening is for these kinds of big, special, real movies.

But you have a one of one legendary filmmaker like Chris Nolan over here with The Odyssey. Then you have someone like Kane Parsons, who made Backrooms, which made a ton of money for A24. I think it was the highest grossing film that they've ever made, and he actually came out and said he would probably make generative AI disappear if he could.

I'm curious about the degree to which you think Hollywood executives care about a young filmmaker, with nascent influence and nascent clout, having something to say about that. Do they give a shit?

They give a shit in the sense that studios are ultimately in the business of talent relations. They want to appeal to the kinds of people that Kane Parsons represents. The whole reason Christopher Nolan made The Odyssey and Oppenheimer with Universal Pictures was because he was at Warner Bros. for many years, and he woke up one morning in 2020 and all of their movies had been put on HBO Max.

The CEO at the time said, “Because of the situation of the world right now, all of the 2021 movies are gonna be put day and date on HBO Max.” That was an example of the CEO thinking tech forward, “We’re gonna give the consumer what they want. We're going to build our streaming service, even if it means grossing less at the box office.”

And the number one filmmaker in town took his talents down the street. They would love to have the next Chris Nolan movie, but instead, Universal, which didn’t do that, they got the number one filmmaker, and they have an amazing relationship with him.

So I think to the extent that studios care about talent, and A24 in particular very much cares about talent, because they are not only appealing to those filmmakers as a business, they have a brand.

A24 is a brand among people who care about movies, and this Google deal, they took a hit for that. People didn't like it. Their fans did not like it. If that ultimately comes back to bite them, and they sell fewer A24 hats or scented candles or whatever's in their merch store today …

Please tell me they have scented candles.

Oh, they do. I got my podcast producer one of them.

And?

He said it smelled nice.

All right, good. Good for them.

But that's where the studios care. Now, is it gonna stop them? No. They have a fiduciary responsibility to their shareholders to bring down the cost of movies, and they see it as an evolution. You know, if you ever see the movie Babylon—there were a lot of people in Hollywood that were very apprehensive about sound in movies because it wiped out a whole generation of silent movie stars who had terrible voices and couldn't articulate themselves. Brad Pitt in that movie is a perfect example.

Then there were people that didn’t like television. They thought it would kill the business, and the VCR, and digital, and streaming. All the different technological advancements that have upended Hollywood, the studios see AI as another one of those, and that if they manage it correctly, it can lead to more profitability, and, in their mind, more movies and TV shows.

Do you agree with that thesis?

That's the big question. I think it needs to be managed properly, because if they go all in and all of a sudden the NBC fall lineup is a bunch of AI slop …

Right.

I think you lose the differentiator. AI is gonna be everywhere on social media, and you know better than anyone that the tech companies are going all in on it, and you're not gonna be able to distinguish what’s real and what's not real online.

So in the future, if you watch a movie like The Odyssey and you see dolphins coming out of the water, you're gonna think that's real if the studios manage that right. And it was real in that movie. They happened to shoot on a day when dolphins were beside the boat, and they got a great shot of dolphins jumping up out of the water.

And that to me is the differentiator that the Hollywood studios still have, and I would hope that they won’t squander it in pursuit of lowering costs.

I want to get to the labor question in all of this. You talked about animation being a place that's very ripe for this kind of disruption. For animation and everything else in Hollywood, to what extent will unions be able to safeguard the rank and file where AI and job loss is concerned?

We've seen it come up as an issue in labor negotiations twice now, back in ’23 and then this past year as well. [Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists] is not against AI. They will tell you openly, “We are not against the use of AI. We are against the use of AI that causes job loss for our members.”

If you use a synthetic performer in a movie, there is a fee paid that makes it just as costly as using a human actor. So it’s not like, “Let’s populate our movie with AI avatars and save money.” For the Writers Guild, if there is a script on which AI is used, there is going to be a credited writer.

AI cannot be the author of a script for the purposes of a guild-covered movie. And that’s important, because ultimately, what are unions? They are for preserving jobs, and they recognize the technology is out there, but they don’t want it to be a replacement. That’s where it gets to the below-the-line union, and it’s much more difficult, because some people are covered, some jobs are covered, some jobs are not covered.

Some are members of the Teamsters. Some are members of IATSE, which is a below-the-line union for various roles in the business. There are lots of jobs on animated movies that are not union-covered, and those are the ones that I think are the most vulnerable. I’m not prepared to go all the way to what Jeffrey Katzenberg said a few years ago, where he said something like 80 percent or 90 percent of the workforce on an animated movie will be replaced by AI.

I don't think that's gonna be the case, at least not for a while, but they are going to eliminate—they already are. They already are eliminating jobs and automating things.

I wanted to ask you about what some have called an emerging gray market. We did a story about this. We published an essay by a woman who was a screenwriter and started finding work training AI models.

I read that.

I thought it was a very funny piece. I thought it was a little bit sad and dystopian, but this idea was that she is basically training herself out of a job. How much do you hear about that happening, that Hollywood workers who are underemployed for a variety of reasons are actually training AI to make a living, regardless of the stigma attached to the technology?

I mean, to their knowledge or without their knowledge? Because you could argue that every screenwriter is training AI because the tech companies are scraping at will.

We’re gonna get to copyright, but I guess a little bit of both, right?

That was an interesting essay, because I had not heard about that happening. I’m sure it does happen. I’m sure that there are jobs out there where you are essentially inputting different scenarios and inputting different types of conversations in order to train AI. I don’t think that’s super prevalent right now, but on the other side of it, there is a widespread fear, in my opinion, in the screenwriting community that the work of screenwriters is being used to train these models without their consent.

But isn’t that fear totally well-founded? I mean, hasn’t it been established that obviously all of that work, if it’s public, would’ve been ingested by a model?
