Yes, but there’s a difference. Well, first of all, I don’t think if you asked Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, on the record, “Do you do this?” they would say yes. Have you actually asked them?

We’ve asked them about how their data sets are trained. I mean, they’re trained on the open web.

Right. But for the most part, most finished movies are not. You’d have to go to piracy.

I see what you mean.

Certainly there are no databases where you can just get every single movie screenplay. Now, there are script databases that you could probably access, but I don’t believe every script that’s ever been written is on the internet.

As we're talking, they must be listening to this and thinking, “What an opportunity for us if we have not yet accessed all of that data.”

Maybe I’m wrong, maybe I’m naive about this stuff. This was a couple years ago, but I asked Aaron Sorkin—I had him for an interview—and I had put a bunch of prompts into ChatGPT and asked it to create a scene of The West Wing set in the Trump White House.

OK.

And it was so bad. It was laughably bad.

They were all sitting instead of walking and talking? What were they doing?

No, they were walking and talking, but it was just generic dialog. It was stuff that didn’t make sense for a character. Like, it just was nonsensical. Maybe that’s improved.

I wanted to ask you about IP and copyright. You used to be an entertainment lawyer, so you are, for many reasons, the perfect person to ask about this. Last year, Disney and Universal sued Midjourney, accusing it of IP infringement because its products could create Shrek or Bart Simpson or Darth Vader. Warner Bros. then joined that lawsuit. Page Six recently called that legal war in its jiujitsu phase, because Midjourney’s …

What does that mean? Is that a fancy word for discovery?

It's a fancy word for “things are getting violent,” maybe. Because Midjourney's lawyers are now demanding that those companies disclose the ways they already use AI.

When you sue someone, you have to know that they’re gonna come for your information, and that’s what you give up when you file a lawsuit: They have access to your documents and communications just like you have access to theirs.

What is your take on that case and on the fair-use issue overall?

So, I have an opinion. But let me first say what the status of the law is, because it’s very unclear. There has not been a definitive determination that using copyrighted material in a model is itself copyright infringement.

The New York Times is in a very expensive legal battle over the same thing.

The better argument for now for these companies to make is that the expression of the output of the model is infringing.

You can take every Disney character and put them into a model, but if what it spits out looks too much like Mickey Mouse, then that itself is infringement, not the ingestion of all of those characters.

Yes, that makes sense.

Now, the entertainment industry would very much like to change that determination and to get courts to rule that the mere act of ingestion is infringement.

We'll see if that ultimately holds water, because it doesn’t look like that's the way things are going. But, you know, there was just this settlement in the book case where a bunch of authors sued, I believe it was OpenAI, it might’ve been Anthropic.

I think it was Anthropic.

It was Anthropic, OK. And the settlement in that one was $1.5 billion.

Yes, it was outrageous.

Yeah, it was not cheap. I think it was the biggest settlement in the history of copyright law, and they’re settling for a reason there. Either the output was too similar or they’re afraid of precedent on the input issue.

It’s going to be fascinating to see how this unfolds over the next five to 10 years, because it’s not clear, and the companies are taking advantage of that vagueness.

Do you have a view here on who should win?

I mean, it’s not going to surprise you that I think that if you put hundreds of millions of dollars into the creation of valuable IP, you should be able to protect that against people who are using it to spit out characters to compete with you.

Sounds entirely reasonable.

Whether that ultimately wins the day, I don’t know, because you have to look at the copyright law framework on this. But to use a fair-use exception to scrape the entire internet, which certainly was not contemplated when the copyright laws were first enacted, I think that’s a stretch.

What about human performers and the idea of voice and likeness? Some are trying to create standards where there aren’t any right now. There's his organization that Cate Blanchett cofounded, RSL Media. The Human Consent Registry is what they have launched, which would be a tool that allows people to control how AI can use their likeness.

Is that the way forward? Is that what we will see more and more of in the future?

I hope so, but that requires buy-in from the various AI companies, and we don't know whether they are going to buy into that. What we have seen is that the entertainment industry is interested in this. CAA, the big talent agency, represents Cate Blanchett. They have thrown their support behind this, and I like that kind of a thing where you have to get consent from a performer or from anyone really to utilize their name, image, and likeness for training models.

SAG-AFTRA has gone in a different direction. They are trying to get a federal right of publicity, because right now this is a hodgepodge of state laws that protect name, image, and likeness.

California has a good one. But if there were a federal right of publicity and an interest in your name, image, and likeness, that would make it easier to protect this federally, and copyright laws are federal laws, obviously.

You've also reported on agencies like CAA and WME meeting with AI companies to basically make deals about their clients’ likeness. What do we know about those deals as they exist now?

Not that much. Do you remember the Tom Cruise–Brad Pitt fight scene?

In what movie?

It was a Chinese model that created a fight scene between Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt.

Oh yes, I remember this. I have an 8-year-old, so I don’t see a lot of movies that don’t involve Moana.

So there was—and this was in the wonderful months when Sora existed …

Oh, yes, an incredible product that so many people wanted.

Especially when you couldn’t use copyrighted images in it. It was really fun when you could make Moana fight Peter Griffin from Family Guy, but then when you couldn't, it was less compelling. So they are trying to have individual meetings with these companies and trying to get a blanket opt-out for all of their clients.

Now obviously, the tech companies, since their inception, have wanted to operate under we will do what we want and you have to opt out, right? The entertainment companies want the default to be opt-out, and if you would like your name, image, and likeness to be included, you can opt in.

That was the big issue with the Zuckerberg AI switch about a month ago. Remember that?

Yes, I do. That actually was a WIRED story.

Yeah, all of a sudden your Instagram photos were gonna be available for anyone to create AI out of.

Unless you knew to go into the settings and tick a button, yeah.

They realized that pissed people off. It’s an ask-forgiveness mentality rather than an ask-permission one.

The entertainment industry would like to change that default. I mean, this goes all the way back to Napster. You have to ask permission, and sometimes permission comes with a fee. So they’re trying to essentially lobby these companies to change the mentality there, and it's an uphill [battle].

I was about to say, there is so much tech money now flooding into Hollywood. Does Hollywood have a shot at this one?

It’s really difficult. I’ll give you a perfect example. The Motion Picture Association is the lobbying group for the studios, and they have a long history. One of their biggest fights over the past 80 years has been piracy, and that’s the big issue they spend all their lobbying and their money on.

So, Sora comes along, right? And you would think this would be a four-alarm fire for the MPA. But guess who’s a member of the MPA now? Amazon.

Of course.

Because they own MGM. So everybody kept asking, “Where’s the statement from the MPA? Where's the statement?” And behind the scenes, Amazon wasn’t going to sign off on an anti-AI-generative-image statement, so they had to go back and forth.

Netflix has mixed feelings about this. We know now that they were talking to Ben Affleck’s company at the time, or were thinking of [it]. So, it’s just a very fraught problem for the industry, because so much tech money is involved. The three biggest buyers of entertainment content right now among the top six are Amazon, Netflix, and Apple.

I have to ask you about Amazon. You have done some phenomenal reporting recently about a Sam Altman film, Artificial, that I am very excited to see but that Amazon MGM suddenly dropped after spending $40 million to make. Tell us more about that mess. How did the movie end up getting made? How did it get dropped, and why?

It's pretty simple. This project was shopped to the market. Amazon was interested in it. It was from a filmmaker, Luca Guadagnino, who they have had a relationship with. He made Challengers for them, and he made a Julia Roberts film last year called After the Hunt for them, and they wanted to do it.

They knew the script. I read the script and wrote about it last summer. At the time I said, “Listen, this is a little dicey, because it’s an indictment of Sam Altman and a scary situation.” It goes into that weekend when the cocreators [of OpenAI] and everybody turned on Sam, and he was kicked out of the company and then essentially got it back and it went on its path …

That was like the Super Bowl for WIRED. That was a wild weekend.

So it essentially dramatizes that event, and nobody looks good except for Ilya. He looks pretty good.

That's really funny.

I've heard from people that that may not …

Yeah, I don't know if that's entirely true, but …

Yeah, but whatever. This is a movie that Amazon wanted to make. They make it, and then all of a sudden in February, it’s announced that they have a $50 billion deal with OpenAI.

They are heavily in bed with that company now. So Mike Hopkins, the head of Prime Video, looks at the finished product. Now, they say the end movie is darker than what they initially envisioned—I haven’t seen the end movie yet; I’ve been told that, yes, it is a dark movie, but that was on the page as well—and they got cold feet.

They essentially ended up paying for someone else to release it. Neon—which is a traditional distributor; they released Anora, the Best Picture winner—they came in, and they got the movie for $0 up front. All they had to do was commit to spending $15 million to release it in theaters, which is what the filmmaker wanted.

Amazon is essentially eating the rest of the cost with the hope that it will become a big box office hit and they will recoup their money, and they did that to get out of this situation, to not have a problem with Sam Altman.

How unprecedented is that? I mean, that is corporate censorship. That is lighting money on fire. That is some real cowardice on the part of Amazon, among other things. That sounds insane to me, but you know this world so much better than I do. How weird is it that that all happened?

It's rare. There was a miniseries about 15 years ago called The Kennedys that was critical of the Kennedy family and was going to be released by A&E, which is half-owned by Disney, and had some connections to the Kennedys, and they voiced their displeasure about it. And that miniseries was offloaded to the Reelz channel, which is an independent cable channel owned by a kind of conservative rich guy.

So that’s an example where that happened. And there's examples all the time where studios just won't touch material because of how hot-button it is.

A perfect example was last year, or two years ago, with The Apprentice, the Donald Trump movie. That was a movie that got a lot of good reviews at Cannes. It wasn't considered great. It was considered good. And the traditional studios just decided that it wasn't worth it. It wasn't worth poking Donald Trump and having a problem for their company. If they did this movie it may find an audience, it may not. It might get some Oscar nominations. It ended up getting two big Oscar nominations for a very tiny distributor, Briarcliff, that had no problem doing this. But that's an example of the studios kind of self-censoring up front. But it's very rare to make a movie and then dump it.

Can Hollywood still take shots at the tech industry? Can they still cover it, or offer versions of those stories with integrity, given how much tech money is now in the industry itself?

It’s a fascinating question. I mean, we’re going to get an answer this fall. Sony is releasing The Social Reckoning, which is Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network, and it’s based on the Facebook Files. That is a very critical story about Mark Zuckerberg. When I interviewed Sorkin, he explicitly connected it to January 6th.

You know, it’s not completely about that, but he makes a direct connection between the decisions that Facebook makes to focus on content that enrages people and divides people to the events of January 6th. So that’s going to be something that I think will be controversial, and Sony is releasing that movie.

Now, Sony doesn’t have a streaming service. Sony is a Japanese company. They also were not one of the companies that settled with Donald Trump. I mean, if you look at what Paramount Skydance has done, they’ve openly courted Trump. You look at Disney with the ABC News settlement with George Stephanopoulos. They paid Trump, I believe it was $15, $16 million.

Those companies were just not even interested in this kind of material. But it’s a great question going forward: How willing is Hollywood going to be to take on the tech industry, either its big moguls or the industry in general.

You’ve done some coverage about astroturfed movie hype. You talked to Lane Brown, who wrote a great piece for New York magazine on this subject. This is the fact that the popularity and virality of movies and TV shows is increasingly manufactured and engineered to seem authentic on social media.

You talked earlier about social media becoming increasingly saturated with AI content, so it’s really hard to figure out what’s real and what’s fake. It’s also really hard to figure out what is authentically good or getting authentic buzz and what is just being paid for by a marketing firm to go viral.

I was curious if you could talk a little bit more about your understanding of that, and if you could offer some advice about how to tell whether something is good anymore.

Amazing question. My rule is: Trust nothing.

Trust nothing.

I did a column about that issue, and I talked to Lane, and I did a pod about it as well, and I had so many of these viral marketers reach out to me saying, “Hey dude, why didn’t you talk to me? I’m pumping out hundreds of thousands of positive and negative tweets every week on this subject. I could’ve told you exactly how I do it.” They’re not shy about it.

If you’re interested in what the new Spider-Man movie is and whether it’s good, and you go on social media, chances are the tweet you see will be paid for. It’s not like that’s an entirely new thing, going all the way back to the beginning of Hollywood and the publicity departments putting out positive stories about the actors and things like that.

But what’s different now is that the algorithms are designed to amplify this kind of content, because the savvy marketers know how to game them and how to include the right words and how to be over the top, and your feeds will be filled up. If you are the kind of person who is interested in Spider-Man content, your feed will be filled up with this kind of stuff.

Both positive and negative. There can be a campaign against a particular actor or movie. The Odyssey stuff is a perfect example. Elon decided he didn’t like it, so it encouraged this whole cottage industry of trolls to whip up anti-Odyssey sentiment. Now, it turns out it didn’t work, and the film was able to overcome that, but a lot of films are not able to overcome that.

My rule is trust nothing, but that’s sort of an easy cop-out. What do you trust? I go to Metacritic.

OK.

If you look at the real reviewers on Metacritic—Rotten Tomatoes is sort of garbage now.

Well, you wrote about PR firms paying critics to artificially boost scores on Rotten Tomatoes, right?

Yeah, Rotten Tomatoes has much more—they would argue inclusive, I would argue democratic—approach to critics. Anyone can be a critic, basically, on Rotten Tomatoes. They have a process to get there, but it’s a lot of people that are, quote-unquote, “awards journalists,” and that means you are pumping up movies to get interviews with the stars.

Metacritic does a better job, I think, of weeding that stuff out, and they also have a 1-to-100 scale. So the thumbs up, thumbs down metric of Rotten Tomatoes is really reductive, because it doesn’t catch the nuance of a review, and often reviews that are mostly negative will be determined to be positive because there’s one line in it that says, you know, “Tom Holland is great,” and that’s what they blurb, and that’s what the review is counted as.

I do use Metacritic, and most of all I don’t trust the buzz on social media at all. A lot of times you’ll see “first reactions” of a movie. Those are all sycophants. Those are bloggers and people and influencers who are invited to a premiere with the expectation that they fawn over the movie afterwards.

Then the trade media picks up on those first reactions and pumps them out as if the movie is amazing. Go look at the first reactions to, like, Supergirl or He-Man or these movies that totally bombed. The first reactions were amazing, because those are the influencers that are essentially paid to be there and treated like kings, and they put out these social media responses that then get aggregated to create a narrative that the studio wants.

Critics are better than that, but even the aggregate critic score, these influencers with agendas make it into those critic scores these days. So you can’t even trust Rotten Tomatoes.

A sad day when we can’t even trust Rotten Tomatoes with our film reviews. That is very disappointing. My husband still uses it all the time. I’m going to have to go home and tell him it’s over.

Metacritic is better. Not perfect, but better.

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

entries.title: How Data Centers Broke American Politics
entries.summary: What the Unabomber, Steve Bannon’s tech guy, and Bernie Sanders taught me about the great data center backlash of 2026.
entries.content:
Joe Allen wants to know what the robot’s name is. At first, I think the double whiskey we downed at the hotel bar must be getting to him, as he sprints like a kid at recess toward a delivery vehicle. I’m anxious about the time: I’m supposed to be driving Allen to the airport, my Hail Mary effort to get him alone for a proper conversation before he leaves Atlanta.

I’ve been back and forth with Allen, who rose to national prominence as the anti-tech prophet on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast, for a few weeks now, seeking an entry into the growing movement against AI. I’d come down to Georgia, a hot spot of data center resistance, to hear one of Allen’s lectures, which he’s been giving at locations across the country. But when I got to the event, he told me he had to leave immediately after.

Fortunately, his flight keeps getting pushed back, which means I can follow him around on various side quests—like this one, to meet some friends at a nearby restaurant. He manages to evade most of my questions about their identities, changing the topic to more interesting things, like the “inverse singularity” (his idea that humanity will approach a point where our intellect and creativity collapse as we rely increasingly on AI for information). Allen’s friends at the restaurant have similarly little information about me, it seems. On our way, one of them calls Allen to ask for an ETA. “I’m bringing a friend—well, a frenemy,” he says, giving me a dramatic side-eye.

There are delivery robots all over downtown Atlanta, one of a handful of major metropolitan areas where they’re being rolled out to bring people burgers or tacos. Allen catches up to this one—which, I’m alarmed to see, has luminous white lights shaped like eyes on its front—and reads a name off the side: “CJ.” I think of the title of Allen’s recent book, Dark Aeon: Transhumanism and the War Against Humanity, and wonder what happened to the delivery worker that this robot replaced. Its eyes look pathetically, limply, past me.

When people ask what I’m doing in Georgia, I give them something easy. People hate data centers, I say, so I’m trying to figure out if they hate AI too. That’s all true. But the topic has also consumed me. In all my years of reporting on energy and the environment, I have never seen anything like the type of vitriol leveled at data centers, or the near-religious fury that has built up around their construction, or the way this resistance seems to be uniting people from the complete opposite ends of the political spectrum.

As I’m writing this piece, a friend sends me a post from a “white Christian nationalism” account on X: a seemingly AI-generated cartoon of Smokey Bear standing in front of a burning data-center-like structure, with the text “ONLY YOU CAN PREVENT DATA CENTERS.” What is happening? my friend asks. I’ll try to explain.

Once upon a time, you may have been living next to a data center and never heard anything about it.

For the past few decades, data centers have been quietly built all over the US, largely in areas with both fiber connectivity and proximity to power—Silicon Valley and the DC area were popular choices. They helped stream Netflix or store stuff in the cloud or do any one of the countless stupid and important things we all do constantly online.

Then came ChatGPT and the AI race. Suddenly, tech oligarchs argued, we needed to build as many data centers as possible—and fast. Making the best AI, they said in speeches and news interviews and social media posts, required a massive buildout, especially of hyperscalers—behemoth versions of the structures we already had. The Trump administration bought in, rolling back environmental regulations to get the government out of the way of development.

Data centers began cropping up everywhere, as companies hurried to find the cheapest land, power, and water. Every day brought a splashier headline. Elon Musk reportedly trucked in unpermitted gas turbines to his Memphis xAI campus, located in a majority-Black neighborhood already suffering from high levels of pollution and contamination. A popular (later disputed) Washington Post article estimated that a single ChatGPT search guzzled the equivalent of a bottle of water. People eyed their electric bills as new data center loads caused utilities to forecast sky-high demand. If you trusted various economic outlets, data center construction now underpinned pretty much the entire US economy. All of this as tech CEOs publicly mused about how AI would take everyone’s jobs and replace human creativity itself.

People, naturally, started to ask questions.

Data center resistance certainly has some of its roots in classic NIMBYism: Lots of Americans simply don’t trust stuff being built, in their backyards, by powerful companies for mysterious purposes. But the pace of the outrage that’s built up around the country is shocking. A recent Gallup poll showed that 70 percent of Americans would somewhat oppose or strongly oppose data center construction in their area. In the past few months, we’ve seen an attack on a pro-data-center council member (Indianapolis’ Ron Gibson); an attack on a tech CEO (OpenAI’s Sam Altman); data center moratoriums introduced in at least a dozen states (including Georgia) and passed in one (New York); and countless cities and counties passing their own bans or moratoriums, including in deep-red places like Hill County, Texas. People have been either arrested, detained, or escorted out while protesting data centers at public meetings in New Jersey, California, Wisconsin, and Indiana.

When I started reporting on data centers last year, Washington was, seemingly, completely unprepared for the backlash. It was unprepared for anything AI-related, really—small wonder for a Congress full of folks so old they can barely work their phones. Two of the first national politicians who I saw call out data center development were the right-wing populists Marjorie Taylor Greene and Thomas Massie, who worried about how a proposed 10-year ban on state-level AI regulations could be leveraged to build data centers on private property. “Forcing eminent domain on people’s private properties to link the future Skynet is not very Republican,” Greene tweeted in June 2025.

Meanwhile, Steve Bannon, Trump’s erstwhile former adviser and a longtime critic of technology, was regularly addressing AI on War Room under Allen’s guidance. At the end of 2025, when the Trump administration tried to re-up a ban on regulation, a MAGA coalition, led by Bannon, was the one to stop it. Bannon told ABC News last fall that Allen was a key part of his plan: “He’s going to every conference possible, meeting people ... and I told him, I want you to go to every church that asks you. I want you to go to MAGA, Tea Party meetings. I want to get the base in the loop on this at the ground floor.”

Anger against data centers and public anxieties about AI are usually treated in polling and policy as separate topics: one an expression of environmental and civic worries, the other concerns about job loss and chatbots. But there's growing evidence that it's not so clear-cut. Research published in June of a small sample size of voters, for example, shows that very few people opposed to data centers actually live near them, and most of those who are against data centers are also skeptical of AI. Bannon, it seems, did a better job reading the room about how the American right might rebel against data centers, airing one segment last year that described data centers as “weapons labs” that are “being turned onto the population.”

I couldn’t shake the feeling that the populist right knew something I didn’t—about AI, about Americans’ attitudes to tech and the built environment. Even about where we might be going with all of this. That’s why, back in January, I first reached out to Allen.

Joe Allen has startlingly blue eyes behind professorial glasses and the shit-eating grin of the guy in high school who likes to tell non-PC jokes. He also has an origin story that’s catnip to lamestream media journalists like me. (And to less lamestream ones, apparently: When I ran into Allen at an event in New York, he was accompanied by Suzy Weiss from the Free Press, who informed me that she was also profiling Allen.) After touring internationally for years as a rigger for musical acts like the Black Eyed Peas and Calvin Harris, with a brief pause to get a master’s in theology from Boston University, Allen watched the music industry collapse during Covid. He’d been writing about the evils of technology, a long-standing interest of his, for far-right and far-left outlets, and he was living in a van in 2021 when Steve Bannon’s producer called to invite him on War Room; Bannon offered him a job as a tech correspondent shortly afterward. At one point, Allen was living at the apartment in DC where War Room is recorded.

The world of AI safety and ethics is incestuous, almost completely inaccessible to normies, and full of people who live mostly in London or the Bay Area. (Many high-profile AI safety researchers, in fact, are headquartered in one office block in Berkeley.) They all argue with each other about whether we’re going to be annihilated by an all-knowing superintelligence and should therefore slow down or halt AI development, or whether that same superintelligence will lead us to Nirvana and should therefore be developed as fast as possible.

Allen arrived in this world as an outsider, able to speak its nerdy language with a mass-appeal, conspiracy-tinted flair. Since his book on transhumanism was published in 2023, Allen has interviewed AI critic Gary Marcus, debated futurist Max More and tech ethicist Nell Watson, and given a talk with a top official from the Golden Gate Institute for AI. The same day that Max Tegmark, an AI safety scholar and the leader of the Future of Life Institute, did an event with Bernie Sanders, he appeared on War Room with Allen and Bannon. The AI safety people began posting about Allen “in all their group chats,” one AI advocacy organization staffer told me. “Now everybody’s like, Joe! Joe! Joe!”

In late 2025, the Center for AI Safety recruited Allen to advise a bipartisan group on AI safety, dubbing it “Humans First,” a term Allen had been using as a kind of rallying cry. The organization’s goal was to figure out how to galvanize regular people around AI, to demand that politicians in Washington put guardrails on a technology that threatens to potentially upend the existence and purpose of humanity. (No pressure.) The event that brought me to Georgia was the second leg of Humans First’s maiden voyage, fresh off a few stops in Florida.

A motley audience filled about half a lecture hall at Georgia Tech that evening. Some were students, including members of a nascent AI safety club that had invited Allen. (Two told me they’d come only because of the posters put up around campus.) A camera guy from More Perfect Union, the leftist content channel that’s become a central hub for anti-data-center videos, hung around filming. Also in attendance was a well-heeled group of Atlantans in their thirties: two women with glossy, long hair and, seemingly, their partners.

Up front, Jeremy Ornstein, a slight Humans First staffer with wild hair, started us off. Like a surprising number of Humans First staffers, Ornstein has a background in climate organizing. It showed: “A tiny group of people in control are racing ahead faster than ever with power and profit,” he warned, in a familiar, almost Obama-style cadence.

Then Allen, sporting a belt with a big American flag buckle, strode up with a “Howdy, Georgia.” He stood before a whiteboard on which, earlier that day, he’d doodled a little Jetsons-style robot, a cheerful expression on its face as it aimed what looked like a ray gun at a group of stick figures with dazed expressions on their faces. “HUMANS FIRST,” Allen had written in big bubble letters, underlined four times.

Allen played clips of Sam Altman intercut with footage of Marshall Applewhite, the leader of Heaven’s Gate. He told us, in his booming east Tennessee drawl, that Heaven’s Gate believers are a good metaphor for what AI leaders believe: Humanity must leave behind our physical bodies to ascend to the heavens, to meet the superintelligent beings living on the other side of the Hale-Bopp Comet. Everyone laughed a little nervously.

Allen’s lectures follow a familiar pattern: jarringly right-wing talking points (at Georgia Tech, a Great Replacement joke!) smashed together with hallucinogenic nightmare descriptions of our future (the idea that a globalist cabal of tech oligarchs want to replace all of humanity with robots). A lot of it can sound completely insane, until you remember: Oh, right. Elon Musk does own a brain-chip implantation company. Sam Altman has blogged about how humans will “be the biological bootloader for digital intelligence and then fade into an evolutionary tree branch.”

“Even if they were to create machines that were smarter than you, even if they created machines more powerful than you, you would have to continue to fight, because if you don't, you're a weakling,” Allen told the room. “If you don’t, you lay down and let the machine roll over you like a monster truck in a white-trash arena, and no one, no one wants that. No one but the most masochistic person wants that.” I found myself, surprisingly, suddenly, on the same page. Yeah! Hell yeah!

Allen ended the speech with a cri de coeur: “To the greenies in the room, I say, Earth first! Right? Greenies?” (Not sure if that was directed at me.) “To the patriots in the room, I say, America first! And for anyone in the room with blood pulsing in their veins, anyone in the room with fire in their minds and hearts, you have to remember, in a machine age, humans first.” I nearly leaped to my feet.

The “friends” Allen is now dragging me to meet turn out to be the well-dressed Atlantans I spotted at the talk, whom Allen had also just met. As he and I chase robots and drink whiskey before joining them, I ask if he has any nice memories of technology. He rattles off a couple typical alt-Gen-X-kid experiences: looking at Jane’s Addiction and Marilyn Manson’s websites; visiting a nascent Rotten.com. But the real shining moment in his relationship with the internet, Allen says, was discovering Ted Kaczynski.

In his book, Allen vividly recalls coming across the Unabomber’s manifesto in the late 1990s while “surfing the web” at his community college writing lab. Kaczynski, a brilliant mathematician undone by the failings of the modern world, wrote “Industrial Society and Its Future” while mailing bombs to universities and business executives; The Washington Post and The New York Times were both encouraged to publish the manifesto as a way to make him stop. “Uncle Ted made more sense than any peacenik or techie cares to admit,” Allen writes.

The influence is apparent. On War Room, Allen acts the part of a preacher at the pulpit warning us all of the coming dystopian age. A lot of his work is somewhat adjacent to body horror: What happens to our souls, he wonders, when our bodies and environments are increasingly digitized? I ask him why he thinks people hate data centers. He says: “If you ever see a fetus growing, and you see the brain growing and the neurons forming—it's amazing. Data centers, if you think about them as neurons of the Antichrist, that’s what we’re witnessing. The false messiah.”

As we arrive at the restaurant, Allen’s new “friends” make space at their table and order some bread. One of them is Hannah Cox, a political influencer with more than 100,000 followers on X. Cox’s husband works in tech and, she tells me, has been “completely blackpilled” by the possibility of AI taking everyone’s jobs. Cox herself is “politically homeless” and came to Allen’s talk even though he’s not, she says, someone she’d usually listen to.

Cox and I have very different social media feeds. When I follow up with her later, as the data center furor in Georgia reaches new heights, she tells me that everyone on her timeline seems to have agreed that data centers are being installed to conduct surveillance on the population. “It’s, I feel like, a ubiquitous fear,” she says. “Like it’s almost a bygone conclusion.”

Two days after I drop Allen off at the airport, I drive out to Troup County, about an hour and a half south of Atlanta, to meet with a local activist named Gage Bailey. Although I arrive at the coffee shop 10 minutes early, Bailey is waiting for me. A stack of documents sits in front of him, color-coded in different highlighters, next to a massive iced drink with a bunch of whipped cream piled on top.

Bailey, a Democrat with a degree in environmental science, first heard about data centers coming to town in the spring of 2025, when an acquaintance told him about one that might pop up on land that was formerly used by an industrial plastics developer. There were, he says, next to no public details about the project—how much power it was going to use, how much water it might draw from the local aquifer. He started doing research, compiling a 13-page memo extensively footnoted with primary sources, about the environmental impacts of data centers.

Like many of the earliest folks involved in the movement, much of which has its origins in environmental concerns spread by groups like local Sierra Club chapters, Bailey began networking with fellow environmental advocates, learning to file public records requests by trial and error. Now, he manages a 4,000-person Facebook group and has helped with anti-data-center efforts in neighboring counties. His co-moderator is running for local office as a Democrat on an anti-data-center platform.

There are a surprising number of Gage Baileys across Georgia, and more are rising up each day. National membership in data center opposition groups on Facebook has exploded in recent months, from under 100,000 in December to more than 500,000 by July. They’re not all Earth-hugging lefties. Shortly after I have coffee with Bailey, a woman in nearby Coweta County goes viral on right-wing media sounding the alarm that Georgia Power, the state’s deeply unpopular utility, is using various tactics to destroy her home and set up transmission lines for a data center—seemingly fulfilling Marjorie Taylor Greene’s Skynet prophecy.

Bailey is hardly the type to watch War Room—he’s focused more on the slog of passing local ordinances than on Allen’s nightmarish visions of our robotic future. But as we talk, I wonder how Allen’s statements about tech oligarchs might land with him. Bailey learned last year that Google was the eventual tenant of the nearby data center project. He and some other environmental advocates had one meeting with Google in November, but afterward the tech giant ghosted them. Working with the company is “not going well,” he tells me. (In a statement to WIRED, Jamal Jessie, an Atlanta-based manager of community and workforce development at Google, said the company was focused on “direct, collaborative engagement with local schools, nonprofits, and civic organizations to deliver tangible regional benefits” and had formed a “$1 million partnership” with a local group helping people with their energy bills.) Bailey, who hasn’t been able to find a job in environmental science and works full-time at a convenience store, has a lot of ire for the world’s most powerful corporations trying to build AI in his backyard. “I don’t see a scenario, at least in the immediate future, in which we’re going to be able to trust these tech companies,” he says.

Bailey’s Facebook group is still growing, and there’s been minimal political unrest so far, he says: Right or left, all members are opposed to data centers, and most of them are deeply skeptical of AI. These unlikely coalitions seem to be holding strong outside of Troup County, too. At a recent anti-data-center demonstration in New Jersey, I asked one mask-wearing protester—who told me they use “any” pronouns and are deeply concerned about the “ethics” of AI—about the right-wing influence on the movement. They shrugged uneasily. “Any enemy of my enemy is, at least, my temporary ally,” they said.

After Atlanta, I can’t stop thinking about the Unabomber, so I brush up on his manifesto. I’d forgotten just how much Kaczynski blames “modern leftism”—with its advocacy for gay rights, feminism, and the like—for the “craziness of our world.” (To be fair, he was an equal-opportunity hater, writing that conservatives “are fools: They whine about the decay of traditional values, yet they enthusiastically support technological progress and economic growth.”) For Kaczynski, leftism was an inevitable byproduct of modern society, which pits humans against the natural order of the world and must be resisted.

Kaczynski was, obviously, not someone to be emulated. But the idea that technology has a role in eroding our humanity is not an unpopular one. My girlfriend tells me a story about her high school English class: Her teacher handed out copies of two anonymized essays—one, a neatly organized dissertation about the pitfalls of technology; the other, a screed warning about the end of the world—and asked students to determine which was written by a sane person. The class overwhelmingly picked the essay about technology, and everyone agreed that the author had a great point. It was, of course, a trick question: Both were written by unreliable narrators, and the essay that resonated was an excerpt from “Industrial Society and Its Future.” Twenty years later, Luigi Mangione, who became an internet folk hero after allegedly shooting a UnitedHealthcare executive in late 2024, left a positive review of Kaczynski’s essay on GoodReads. Last year, PCMag—hardly a bastion of leftist anti-tech thinking—published an essay titled “The Unabomber Was Right.” As Allen writes in his book, Kaczynski also left a mark on some high-profile tech thinkers, including Ray Kurzweil, who wrote in 2000 that Kaczynski was “correct on the deeply entangled nature of the benefits and risks” of technology.

There are echoes of Kaczynski, I think, in the resistance to renewable energy. In states like Vermont, it has turned crunchy hippie types against technology like solar and wind, and this resistance is now baked into some of the DNA of the anti-data-center movement. A 2025 study found that more than 450 counties and municipalities across nearly all states had some sort of solar or wind restrictions in place, a 16 percent increase from the year before. The Make America Healthy Again movement, too, can be viewed as an expression of a Kaczynski-esque environmentalism: the idea that modern society is poisoning our land, air, and water and that modern inventions like vaccines or antidepressants are actually bad for us. Many of these ideas can often collide in strange places. Currently, one of the top Substack writers in the site’s Climate and Environment category is a green-living farmer who has gone on the attack in recent months against solar installations in upstate New York, claiming (misleadingly) that the panels can poison the soil and destroy farmland.

Allen’s book is a wilder read than “Industrial Society and Its Future.” The appendix, titled “My 55-Point Plan to Stay Human,” with suggestions like “Say hello to your neighbors” and “Buy a flip phone,” would be a hit at any leftist reading group in 2026 (perhaps with an edit to remove Allen’s insistence on “secure borders”). I agree with his assertion, moreover, that “it’s easy to imagine a day when … the specter of deadly AI is used to clamp down on freedom and erect miserable technocratic systems.” I do not, however, think the Covid-19 pandemic or “climate change” are examples of this already happening. Jennifer Bilek, a prominent anti-trans writer who claims that the medical-industrial complex has “infiltrated” gay and lesbian communities to push “transgenderism,” blurbed Allen’s book. When Allen recommends that I talk to her, I make an offhand remark that I don’t think she’d like me very much. “Oh, right,” he says, wiggling his eyebrows at me and referencing the pronouns listed on my X bio. “‘They/them.’”

Right-wing anti-globalism isn’t the only way to do anti-AI populism, of course. The scholars Timnit Gebru and Émile Torres argue that the development of AI is mostly an excuse for the wealthy and powerful to exploit existing inequalities and push a eugenic agenda. (Gebru and Torres have also criticized AI safety groups, including the Center for AI Safety, which has given money to Humans First.) There’s also the religious way. In May, Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica Humanitas, his encyclical on AI, which advises humanity to develop technology responsibly and always be aware of the primacy of humanity. Like clockwork, a post popped up on my X feed of a photo of the Unabomber split with a photo of Leo. “You killed the man … But not the idea,” the caption read.

Data centers, which are bringing together the most disparate neighbors in all regions of the country, may represent an opportunity to wage a real, unified fight against tech oligarchs. There’s a dream here, evident even in the pages of The New York Times, which in early May ran a headline that called data centers “the most bipartisan issue since beer.” The movement seems to envision a middle ground between rejecting technology wholesale—of truly Unabombering out—and rolling over and giving Big Tech everything it wants. But even if this middle ground does exist, it’s going to be a journey to reach it—one that our political system might not be prepared for.

In the weeks after I return from Georgia, it feels like the mainstream right fully takes over the data center conversation. People like Tucker Carlson and Matt Walsh make viral videos questioning the construction of specific projects. (By the way, Allen specifically wanted me to get this on the record: “Matt Walsh should have his beard plucked out like an Egyptian priest and be forced to kneel before Osiris. He copies my fucking shit all the time.” Walsh, through a spokesperson, disputes this.) Nancy Mace, running for governor in South Carolina, announces that she supports a yearlong moratorium. Florida governor Ron DeSantis, an outspoken AI and data center critic, signs first-of-its-kind legislation to ensure, in part, “that local governments maintain the authority to reject data center development in their communities.”

Politics comes for Humans First too. In late March, there’s a high-profile spat online where pro-AI White House allies like Marc Andreessen and David Sacks retweet a piece critical of Humans First. Shortly after, the organization splits along partisan lines. The conservative wing keeps the Humans First name and makes the right-wing political activist Amy Kremer, who helped organize the January 6 “Save America” rally in DC, its chair; Allen leaves the group. When I ask Allen about the changeup, he is curiously coy (but characteristically body-horrible): The group was “undergoing mitosis,” he says. “I am now a lone organelle floating in the residual cytoplasm.”

In mid-April, I go to DC for a Humans First event billed as the kickoff for the conservative arm. While I’m in town, I have this idea of taking Allen to visit an area of northern Virginia colloquially referred to as Data Center Alley, the densest stretch of data centers in the world, just about an hour outside the city. I reach out to a few operators to see if anyone will let us inside. It’s a weird email to send: I know everyone hates you right now, but could you let me into your facility to reassure everyone it’s not filled with poisonous water and haunted spirits? Almost immediately I receive polite nos. It’s for security reasons, one representative says.

I end up driving around Data Center Alley anyway. (Allen is too busy to come.) I’m prepared to be a little underwhelmed—data centers are, as I’ve told countless people, just buildings. But I’m genuinely shocked by the sheer density of what’s here, how much construction I see, how impossibly big the buildings look edging up on the neatly manicured lawns of the wealthy northern Virginia suburbs. One of them, a Vantage facility partly painted a beautiful deep blue, is so loud that I can hear a constant, low-level hum even in the cul-de-sac across the street. I don’t know it yet, but months from now, Humans First will organize a national day of protest against data centers, with events in nearly 150 counties across 42 states.

I park my car in the cul-de-sac and take out my notes from the night before, on a speech at the Humans First event given by a woman named Alicia Shamblin. Her 23-year-old son, Zane, killed himself last year after drinking hard ciders and talking to ChatGPT for hours; she and her husband are now suing OpenAI. Got his masters’ degree a few months earlier, my notes read. ChatGPT told him “Rest easy, king.” I wonder from which data center the LLM had sent that last message.

entries.title: The Real Story Behind the 2018 Google Walkout
entries.summary: In 2018, more than 20,000 employees walked out to protest how Google handled allegations of sexual harassment. Here’s how they organized it from inside the company.
entries.content:
In 2018, Claire Stapleton was living in New York, raising a young child, and working at Google as a marketing manager. In October of that year, upset with how the company had handled sexual harassment claims, she helped organize what became known as the Women's Walkout. In this new excerpt from her book Don’t Be Evil, she explains how one Google Group helped start it all.

On the Saturday after I started the womens-walk Google Group, I sprang awake at 6 and opened my laptop, stealing time before my son Malcolm stirred. My inbox was dotted with the usual weekend emails from my manager, Marion. We were in the middle of a big push involving Article 13, a piece of EU legislation that would hold platforms liable for user-­generated content. I’d strenuously avoided learning the ins and outs of this particular bit of lobbyist infighting. But the drumbeat went on. “#SaveYourInternet!” we screeched from our Twitter and Instagram accounts, multiple times a day, with slick branded graphics. It was supposedly “top urgency,” despite being both inside baseball and counter to every brand goal we’d set for the year.

I’d been at YouTube long enough to know the truth: If Google wanted this law overturned so badly, Article 13 was probably good for the world. The company didn’t want limits on growth, accountability, or liability; it wanted a frictionless, consequence-­free internet and the endless consolidation of power that came with it.

I couldn’t absorb Marion’s Saturday to-­do list. My mind was consumed by the Women’s Walk. I refreshed the tab where I’d set up the new Google Group. An avalanche of names had joined— only a handful I knew. Most were strangers, and yet their presence felt like a new kind of belonging.

I wasn’t overthinking anything; I was just writing, sending, doing. The energy was right there, primed. I typed an email—from my own account, my name fully attached, come what may.

From: Claire Stapleton Sat, Oct 27, 2018 at 6:46 am

To: womens-­walk

*rolls up sleeves*

welcome to ground zero of the google women’s walkout / a day without women (naming/branding tbd).

couple of open Q’s for the group (200 of us and counting!) as we start to formulate the statement of purpose and next steps:

what do you hope this collective action accomplishes (could be what we express/communicate to leadership, could be an action leadership agrees to take, could be a more existential cultural change we set into motion)? put another way:

why are you here?

thoughts on when we should do it? mindful of giving us enough time to make this as global, inclusive, and big as we can while also capitalizing on the rage-­buzz-­momentum we have flowing right now. there’s also the US midterms (a week from Tuesday) to consider.

please forward to friends who’d be interested in getting involved.

–claire

Replies shuffled in all weekend. People wrote under their real names; the anonymity cloak was gone. The I’m so fucking mad emails gave way to discussions of culture, then strategy. We made our first decision almost immediately: The walkout would be Thursday, November 1—just five days away. The US midterms were November 6; waiting would dilute everything, especially our greatest asset: rage.

What followed was a week at Google unlike any other. Here’s how it unfolded.

The Walkout was all I wanted to work on, but there was the usual rigmarole first. Article 13 had momentarily faded, so we pivoted to a slate of uninspired Halloween tweets—special-­effects makeup tutorials, a stop-­motion pumpkin. The contrast between that bullshit and the walkout planning—with its electricity and urgency as women across Google convened—was almost psychedelic.

A project manager named Tanuja reached out and offered to help. We met in a conference room in my building; she was hyper-­organized, fired up, ready to project-­manage the hell out of this. In 45 minutes, we outlined a rough plan and built an internal site: a “hub and spoke” model with local leads in every office, each customizing the day with their own stories and flair.

Tanuja was another good girl pushed to the brink. Rule follower. Devoted worker. And now: ready to step out of line and not care who saw. I left the meeting fortified. This was what solidarity felt like—so different from the solitary, self-­erasing “teamwork” I’d practiced for years.

That night, as I cooked dinner for Malcolm and my husband, Shane, I took a call from a guy named Amr. He’d chimed in to the womens-­walk group with a warning: Yes, we had a legally protected right to organize, but Google would likely push back hard. It was bracing to hear aloud: The company was almost certainly monitoring us, taking note.

Amr described himself as an “entry-­level engineer,” which was a bit of shtick but also refreshing—the rare person at Google who didn’t care about posturing their seniority, calling themselves a “global head” of whatever microscopic-in-the-grand-scheme project they’d been assigned to. He was incredibly knowledgeable and passionate about organizing—he had organized restaurant workers in the South after college with the Fight for $15 movement and had been involved in various activist causes at Google since the day he joined. He referred to management as “the bosses,” a phrase I’d never heard in the company’s Disneyland of techno-­optimism.

He told me we had an obligation to use our privilege to check Google’s power. The directness of that sentence alone was disorienting.

Amr, along with a woman named Meredith Whittaker, had been organizing opposition to Maven, the Department of Defense project that used Google’s AI for drone surveillance and targeting. I’d heard her name for years—she was known as a rare example of actual moral clarity inside Google. We had mutual friends, and she was a fellow Californian who’d joined Google at roughly the same golden-era moment I had.

Meredith had a mane of wild brown curls and dressed in head-to-­toe black, a cross between a philosopher and a downtown artist. She carried a grounded, almost zen steadiness—but sharpened at the edges. She was a serious yoga practitioner, and that same flexibility showed in her mind. Google had even flown her to Mountain View to debate Vint Cerf, the so-called father of the internet, about Maven in front of a live audience of Googlers. She’d built an airtight case for why Google had no business building the machinery of war—why a company supposedly founded on “Don’t be evil” could not, in good conscience, lend its algorithms to lethal systems. Vint, for his part, gave the classic techno-utopian line about technology being a neutral tool like a hammer. It landed like a damp paper towel. She wiped the floor with him. People were still talking about it.

Meeting Meredith and Amr felt like discovering a subterranean conscience under the Google I’d known—a network of people who had been resisting and organizing. And I couldn’t help thinking: Where was all this while I was quietly drowning, trying to grapple with the moral dissonance of my work alone?

Amr was openly skeptical of us doing a walkout—it was too big, too fast, even if he had to concede the train had already left the station. One of his organizing maxims was that you have to know where people are: politically, emotionally, and—most crucially—what they’re willing to risk. Traditional organizing, he said, starts at one lunch table and spreads sideways from there. You build tight bonds, real solidarity, because when things get hard—and they will—you need people who will stand with you. There were no shortcuts.

And yet, we had momentum. People were G-chatting me constantly, offering support, asking how they could get involved.

But Amr’s questions stuck with me. Why was everyone so fired up now? What exactly were they reacting to? I wanted to understand the contours of that rage.

So on Monday night, I emailed the listserve with a simple prompt and a Google Form: “Why are you walking out?”

We got 350 responses.

Here are a few:

My director pressured women into wearing high heels regularly and openly, pressured overweight women on the team to “hit the gym, be athletic,” and referred to our clients as “battered women” because they “keep coming back” regardless of how we treat them. He required that we walk a certain speed around the office. He told a joke one morning to the managers only that my manager repeated to me: his son had asked him what being gay meant. He told him, “it’s when a boy wants to be a girl.” At team outings, he’d routinely refer to anyone not drinking as “pussies.” He referred to the only African American person on the team as “dark horse.” He said in a 1:1 that he believed many men on the team “had small dicks.”

There was an off-­site at a resort. During the off-­site, the director and the team, including his ABP [associate business partner a.k.a. assistant], were having drinks. There were a few male non-Googlers at the resort as well that they hung out with. The ABP retired for the night. The director facilitated, somehow, getting the ABP’s room key into the hands of the non-­Googlers, who were all very inebriated. The non-­Googlers entered her room while she was sleeping and attempted to climb into bed with her. She successfully kicked them out of the room without being attacked. What followed was an official HR investigation across the org. Two men on the team lied to HR to try and cover up any wrongdoing from the director. It’s unclear whether they did this on their own or were pressured from the director to lie. Shortly after the investigation, the ABP left the company. I was instructed by my former manager to never report anything to HR in order to protect myself and my career, and I believed her and continue to believe her. The director has since been promoted 3 times.

I was working on a Google UK team with a terrible “boys club” culture. One day the women came in and the boys had left to go do a stereotypical “male” sports activity. We were horrified that we hadn’t been included or informed. Due to my persuasion, we wrote a letter to HR. Nothing happened. The next day, the manager called the women into his office 1 by 1, all younger women than me, and he was furious. Every one of them came out crying, regretted writing the letter, and said they would never interact with HR again, and that we should never have said anything. I felt so ashamed I had brought this on them.

When I took a sick leave and came back, my manager did not want to work with me and asked me to leave his team. He said if I stayed longer my performance ratings were going to drop. I went to the VP, several senior folks in the team and did not get support. HR investigated the case and talked to 2 folks who were not even connected with the case and closed it. As part of the investigation they told me that the manager acted in bad taste but due to Business needs his decision was right. During this process I found another role. Since I found a job, they said they were not taking action. Also as part of closing the investigation they threatened that if I talk to anyone about this I will be terminated. The Manager is still at Google, has harassed or treated several more women on his team badly. He’s been promoted multiple times.

I’m a woman of color. I was underleveled and took a 20% pay cut when I joined Google. After 3 years, and 2 successful promotions, I’m finally going to be making the same base salary as I did prior to working at Google (but inflation and cost of living changes will still render me worse off). I am in HR. I come to work and fight for fairness and improvement for Googlers every day. Who is fighting for me?

It was a stunning, sobering monument of disillusionment, capturing all sorts of anecdotes and reflections on a culture of discrimination, gaslighting, retaliation, ethical breaches, punitive managers, bad HR. If I could boil all these responses down to a single question, it might be: When did you first notice the gap between what you believed Google to be—progressive, equitable, fair, good—and what you actually see and experience every day?

I kept the tab open and read them as they came in, one by one, clicking back to the tab all day as I did other stuff. As I look back now, it’s so clear to me this was the turning point. I came up the ranks as a corporate storyteller, a buoy of the company narrative. The foundation of that work, the frame of it, is the belief that telling Google’s story would help usher in a better world. Some people have always understood that was bullshit, or propaganda. But you can’t really do the work if you think that way. You have to believe, as I did, that Google (and all technology companies) is essential to progress, is making the world a better place.

But now it was undeniable: Those stories, those narratives, those “values” were doing the opposite. They were a veil, cover, PR glossing over the rot.

And what was Google’s business really adding to the world, at the end of the day?

Ads. A surveillance empire. The scaffolding of attention capture and influence. We would make people’s stories—the real ones, not the sanitized internal versions—the centerpiece of the walkout.

Maybe, like Christine Blasey Ford’s story, they wouldn’t topple anything. But they could puncture the myth. And, I realized, sometimes that’s where real change starts.

entries.title: Mistral Is in the Right Place at the Right Time
entries.summary: Open-weight AI models are having a moment in the wake of recent turmoil at US tech giants. For French AI lab Mistral, that’s the the best thing that could have happened.
entries.content:
Mistral is having a moment. With access to less funding and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, the French AI lab has lagged behind its American rivals in model performance. But recent turmoil stateside has created a window of opportunity.

In June, the Trump administration placed restrictions on the distribution of models from Anthropic and OpenAI, giving Europe a glimpse of an unwelcome future in which its access to bleeding-edge AI could be suddenly revoked. A few weeks later, one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked multiple companies; Anthropic then revealed that its models had engaged in similar behavior. The incidents revived a long-running debate over safety risks tied to proprietary, closed-weight models, whose inner-workings are a closely guarded secret.

Mistral frames itself as the antidote: a Europe-based alternative to the American labs, whose models—most of which are published under an open source license for anybody to use—cannot escape scrutiny or be switched off unilaterally.

“If you don’t end up in a situation where most people are building open source, you’re giving way too much power to companies that are going to become statelike—that will behave in a very aggressive way to make sure that nobody can compete,” Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch told a packed room at an AI conference in Paris last month. “The alternative to open source winning is actually a pretty dark world.”

Mensch’s argument is self-serving but effective. Last September, Mistral raised almost $2 billion at a $13.5 billion valuation; it's reportedly teeing up another raise that will bump that figure to $23 billion. The lab’s revenue has reportedly increased 20-fold in the past year, helped along by deals with the French government, Microsoft, HSBC, and others.

“The continental strategy of the EU to become more technologically sovereign … and the increased hostility of the US is a magic formula that all of a sudden puts Mistral—whose performance has not been spectacular—in a favorable position,” says Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies.

Mistral has long believed the AI market would be too large to be controlled by any single country without causing geopolitical instability, Mensch says. “It’s comparable to energy—electricity,” he told WIRED in an interview after the conference. “You want to make sure that you have security of supply, diverse ways of sourcing the technology, so that nobody can turn you off.”

That case has become easier to make since the US government, with the return of Donald Trump to the White House, began to demonstrate a willingness to leverage its domestic capabilities against trading partners. “More and more, AI is understood as a major vector of power,” Mensch told WIRED. “The new administration makes everything a little more emotional.”

The recent surge in the adoption of open-weight models is part of that picture. One of few ways that European businesses can guarantee undisrupted access to AI, Mensch argues, is to run open-weight models on domestic infrastructure. “Everybody outside the US and China should participate in the open source ecosystem, because it takes leverage away,” says Nicolas Granatino, founder of startup accelerator StemAI, who holds a stake in Mistral in a personal capacity.

Until fairly recently, it was unclear how to monetize open-weight models effectively, according to Granatino. Unlike the leading American labs, locked in a race to superintelligence, Mistral has shifted its focus toward smaller, bespoke models for manufacturing, utilities, and financial services. It has also developed a cloud business through which customers can access its models, and a Palantir-style team of engineers who embed within client organizations. “At the moment, we see the emergence of a product that is making the open source commitment easier,” says Granatino. “You can make money running the infrastructure” and help clients to customize models with their own data.

Meanwhile, the American labs that charge a premium for access to their proprietary models are finding that their performance advantage is being continually eroded by distillation, the process of training a lesser AI model on the outputs of a more capable model. “That seems like it’s always going to be difficult to stop,” says Neil Lawrence, a professor of machine learning at the University of Cambridge. For companies whose business is structured around open source, like Mistral, distillation isn’t so much of a problem, because anybody can access and build atop their open-weight models to begin with.

Whether Mistral has arrived at this juncture through foresight, blind good fortune, or a combination of both, the stranglehold of the American labs is beginning to loosen as more businesses turn to open-weight models. Though gaps in publicly available data confuse the picture, the market share of open-weight models appears to be rising steeply, driven by rapid growth in the adoption of Chinese models, like DeepSeek, in particular.

“We revealed to the world that you could actually build AI systems outside the control of US labs,” Mensch says. “That is now changing the structure of the market itself.”
